EUROPEAN. ( London Weekly Dispatch, July 15.) One of those terrible wars of extermination which spring up between tribes hostile in leligion is raging in Syria. The Druses, worshippers with their own fanaticism and their own mysteries, yet. strongly imbued with some portions of the creed of Mahomet, are slaughtering the Maronites, Christians of an independent Church, long accustomed to the protection of France as the guardian of all the Latin interests in the Levant. The details are horrible, and exact interference in the cause of common humanity. Most rejoiced are we to see that Fiance and England arc takings conceited course by sending a part of their Mediterranean fleets to the coasts to stop the carnage if possible. But it must not be supposed that the injmies are all on one side. It is a case of hereditary, inextinguishable religious feud, of hate falsely consecrated on both tides by the evil authority of dogma. Let such as doubt what theological ferocity can prompt in India see, thus much nearer, what it perpetrates. We read in a letter from Beyrout, via Paris, that þÿ the Maronites have fora long time been excited by the Jesuits to invade the districts inhabited by the þÿDruses. We notice this in no desire to cool any zeal for the protection of those now in danger of becoming victims, but to show what the true remedy is, that the contending fanatics shall be made to acknowledge the irresistible authority of a civil power, and shall be compelled by equal laws, fairly administered, to respect rights common to every human

society. Whether Turkey can afford a protection of j this kind is unhappily more than doubtful. The Emir Beschir, deposed for favouring Mehemet Ali, when the latter endeavoured to possess himself of Syria as an appendage to Egypt, j achieved something of that kind in the Asiatic form, quelling ferocity by inhumanities yet more j teeming press of Dentu, terrible. The poor effete creature that nominally reigns at Constantinople, but really sells his power for the enjoyment of an unbounded levy from the public purse, and whose chief exercise of Royalty is exhibited in his personal luxuries, certainly will never show the stiong baud that can compass such murderous disseusion. It is

the encroachments of France and Russia, and keep open the road to India. If so, we are in a false position, one which, in this searching age, when nothing has the mark of endurance that cannot also show the mark of right, is a serious danger to us. Far better that another Congress should be called ; that the populations which compose the Turkish empire should be established in separate territorial rights; that a general guarantee, which would be at least ns powerful as that which upholds the present state of established anarchy, should protect the independence

open to a dispute at the most inopportune time, when a strong despotism will be the only substitute for a despotism that lias rotted out. It is a condition of things without example that a tyranny over many unwilling nations, an authority utterly unable to exist by itself, should be upheld by a compact of other Powers. It adds to the marvel of unrighteousness when the only motive of the agreement is the mutual dread of the alien oonspiriug parties. We know well tho complications of the subject. As others have doubtless done, we have reasoned them by ourselves over and over again to their no-conclusion. Of this only are we perfectly sure, that while England defends the communications of her empiro against the ever envious and malicious agents of her rivals, she must utterly get rid of the reproach of maintaining outrageous misrule, or no rule, for her own purposes, and must enforce a chance for the people of the East to live and die like human beings. It seems as if the great religious hatreds were everywhere drawing to battle. They poison contention in every realm whose convulsions and miseries we have to chronicle. This is a practical libel on Divinity. Tho first lesson the world bas to learn is to restrain the priesthood everywhere to its own office; for wherever it bring religions authority into secnlar affairs, it reduces religion to a selfish idolatry and curses mankind with a practical worship of demons

AUSTRIA. The publication of the budget of the Austrian YVar Department, which has just been made at Vienna, has produced a painful impression. The public are particularly surprised to see 1,000,000 florins set down in it for the troops of the D ike of M 'dena, whom ho took with him fiotn Italy. Thu Austrians say that as the Duke possesses an immense fortune (the greater part of which is invested in the English funds) he ought to pay for these troops, and

not throw the burden of doing so on the Austrian taxpayers who are grievously suffering from the supplementary war taxes, which still continue to be levied. It is believed that the item will be energetically protested against in tbe Council of the Empire.

TURKEY. There is at present a tremendous religious ferment in Bulgaria and Roumelin, and it is by no means unlikely that there will bo a great schism in the Greek Church. In the neighbourhood of Seres no fewer than 20,000 oitliodox Greeks have thrown off' the supremacy of the Patriarch at Constantinople and joined the United Greeks, who recognise the Popo as their spiritual chief. For tbe moment everything is quiet in Servia, and it is believed at Belgrade that the þÿ þÿfaiseurs have received orders from Russia to remain passive for a time. Advices from Constantinople to the 4th instant state that in consequence of the mission of the Grand Vizier, the, agitation in Roumelia and Bulgaria had subsided. The Grand Vizier had visited Belgrade and the eastern provinces. Agitation prevailed at Damascus, and cannon had been placed in position The number of troops was considered insufficient. There was a general panic at Beyrout, and the Christian inhabitants were taking to flight. Turkish reinforcements had arrived.

London Times, July 14. FRANCE. (from the þÿtimes correspondent.) One sees occasionally, in such of the Irish newspapers as seem still inspired by the charlatanism, so itigliiriougly terminated in 1848, fierce invectives against England aud English rule, and thinly-disguised aspirations alter a foreign domination. Thu writers of these effusions do not perceive that, while they denounce the Government which they say oppresses them, they afford the best proof of the liberty they enjoy in the very impunity with which they ate allowed to utter disaffection, aud even downright tteason. They do not see that a Government can hardly be the tyrannical and cruel one they describe which permits the vituperation they indulge in to be repeated in perfect security day after day But they must be lost to all feeling of self-respect or shame, in proclaiming to the world that the Irish people are the most miserable, the most crushed of' all nations on the face of the earth, and by accepting the pamphlets of La Question Irlandaise þÿ and MacMahon Hoi d'lrlande, as the true description of their country. Irishmen abroad, and, I hope, very many at home þÿ Irishmen | and Catholics who can sincerely love their \ country and their creed, must blush with slialne at. those most ignoble libels. They almost wish that this class of patriots were satisfied to the utmost, and that they were for a short space under the rule of a French Marshal. In the meantime, I off r them the following little incident as a sp eimen of the system which Mac

Mahon Roi þÿd frlande would probably inaugurate in the country over which it is desirable he should rule, aud which would no doubt bring it to that quietude which, in the opinion of certain patriots, is the perfection of political and personal liberty. Two or three years ago a man named About þÿ not the pamphleteer þÿ was convicted of some not very heinous offence and sentenced to a certain term of imprisonment, and afterwards to a surveillance of the police. He was forced to reside in a certain district, under penalty if he quitted it, aud thus committed rupture du ban, for further imprisonment of from one to five years. In case of rupture du bun no second trial is necessary ; the fact of being seen out of the district to which lie is limited is of itself sufficient to legally justify punishment. About wns in this po-iti m ; lie quitted the district or department, to which his movements were confined, and his period of surveillance not having expired, he was arrested and imprisoned for one year on tho charge of rupture du bun. Against all this there is no objection, for so is the law. On Monday la-t, however, his þÿyear s imprisonment, which he spent, in the department of the Meurthe, ended, and, in due, e ,urse, he should have been set at liberty, having completed his penalty. He certainly was taken out of the prison of Nancy, not, however, to return to his home, but to bo transported for ten years to Cayenno. Thu Irish þÿ þÿpatriot may ask what was tho offence which brought

ou him so grievous a punishment ? The offence was that, as the prefect of the department, had been informed, he used offensive expressions against the Emperor. Whether this new charge was wi II founded or not does not appear, because he was not (tied, and, of course, not convicted. Tho simple assertion of a police agent was considered sufficient proof of his guilt

But the words attributed to him, even if they were really expressed, were not the twentieth part of the vituperation against the English Government uttered by certain orators and writers in Ireland. The story would not be complete if I did not add that the prefect of the department was, 1 hear, an advanced Republican 10 or 12 years ago, and perhaps One ol M Ledru þÿRobin commissioners. s The following is the mild decree of the 8th of December, 1851, countersigned by M. de Monty, then Minister of the Interior, and now President of the Legislative Corps, and wlrch is embodied in the supplement of the French Code : þÿ þÿ The President of the Republic decrees, þÿ Every person placed under the surveillance of the high police, who shall be recognized ns guilty of rupture du bun, may he transported, as a measure of public security, to a penal colony in Cayenne or Algeria. The term of transportation shall bo for five years at least, and for ten years at most. The same measure shall he applicable to persons teengnized as having formed part of a secret socn ty. þÿ The effect of his being placed under the surveillance of the high police shall be to give to the Government tin- right of fixing on the place in which the condemned party must reside after he shill have completed his punishment. The Administration (the Prefects, &e.) shall determine the formalities necessary to prove the constant presence of the condemned party in the place of his þÿresidence. Until such time as General MacMahon shall

have assumed the crown on the hill of Tara, tho gentlemen w ho yearn for .that, event would doubtless consider it an advantage to be gradually' inducted into the system of administration of which appatently tin y are so enamoured, otto taste a few of the sweets scattered here and theie in the Code on the press. But it is painful to witness so much ignorance ; it is painful to see the contemptuous compassion i f Inieigiiers wlio know no better whenever In land is mention, d, and who take their no ion of Irishmen fia.iu the description Irishmen often give of themselves and their country ; and it is humiliating to find an affectation of a preference f y a system which would soon give a good account of enthusiastic orators and writers ; of men who would so. it find, to their cost, the difference hi tween a Fnneb Ma shut and an English Viceroy.

L. Petersen. Fm. Publication from THE MINISTRY OF FINANCES concerning a further clause to be inserted in licenses issued by the Government of the Danish Westindia Possessions to persons still living to summon their creditors by proclama.

01 ) N a most submissive Minister of Finances, His Majesty the report from the King has under date of 13th instant most graciously sanctioned, that in licenses for the issuing of a proclama summoning creditors, which are henceforth granted ad mandatum by the Government for the Danish Westindia Possessions to persons during their life-time, it shall be provided, that the notice to creditors shall gi\ e a year and six weeks warning, to be reckoned from the time that such proclama has been recorded in the Royal Upper Court in Copenhagen and in the Upper- and Lowercourts in the Danish Westindia Possessions and has, three times consecutively, been published in the Berling political and advertising gazette, the St- Croix Avis and the St. Thomae Tidende, and otherwise with the clauses hitherto observed according to the Placard 20th February 1717, I. A, $ 18 and the Chancery Letter of 28th November 1789. Which according to the Royal Authorisation given me, is hereby made known for the observation of all concerned. Ministry of Finances, Copenhagen, 19th June 1860. FENGER.
L. Petersen.

Lord Palmerston knows me, and when I affirm a thing he will believe me. Well, you can tell him from me, in the most explicit manner, that since the peace of Villafranca 1 have had but one thought, one object þÿ to inaugurate a new era of peace, and to live on the best terms with all my neighbours, and especially with England I had renounced Savoy and Nice; the extraordinary additions

to Piedmont alone caused me to resume the desire to see reunited to France provinces essentially French. But it will be objected þÿ You wish for pence, and you increase, immoderately, the military forces of þÿFrance. I deny the fact in every sense. My army and my fleet have in them nothin! of a threatening character. My steam navy is even far from being adequate to our requirements, and the number of steamers does not nearly equal that of sailing ships deemed ti-cessary in the time of King Louis Philippe 1 have 400,000 men under arms ; hut deduct from this amount 60,000 in Algeria, 6,000 at Romo, 8,000 in China, 00,000 gendarmes, the sack, and tile new conscripts, and you will see þÿ vhat is the truth þÿ that my regiments are of smaller effective strength than during the preceding reign. The only addition to the army List has been made by the creation of the Imperial Guard. Moreover, while wishing for peace, 1 desire also to organize the forces of the country on the be.-t possible footing, for, if foreigners have only seen the bright side of the last war, myself, close st. hand, have witnessed the defects, and I wish to remedy them. Having said thus much, I have, since Villafranca, neither done, urr even thought, anything which could alarm any one. When Lavalctte started for Constantinople, the instructions which l gave him were confined to this þÿ Use every effort to maintain the status quo ; the interest of France is that Turkey should live as lung as þÿpossible. þÿ Now, then, occur the massacres in Syria, and

it is assented that 1 am very giad to find a new occasion of making a little war, or of playiug a new part. Really, people give me credit lor very little common sense. If I instantly proposed an expedition, it was because my feelings were those of the people which has put me at its head, and the intelligence from Syria transported me with indignation. My first thought, nevertheless, was to conic to an understanding with England. \\ hat other interest than that of humanity could iuduce þÿ strength Cau 1 conceal tioin myself that Al- he that the possession of it would increase my me to send troops into that country f þÿ . Could it geria, notwithstanding i s future advantages, is a souice of weakness to France, which for 30 years has devoted to it tile purest of its blood and its gold I I said it in 1852 at Bordeaux, and my opinion is snil the þÿsame 1 have great conquests to make, bit only in France. Her interior organization, (ter moral development, the increase of fu r ne-nurees, have still immense progress to make. þÿ here I a field exist vast enough for my ambition and sufficient, to satisfy it. li was difficult for mo to come to an understanding with England on the subject of Central þÿlia y, because 1 was bound by the peace of Vilafranca. As to Southern Italy. I am Ircc from engagements, and l ask no better than a concert with England on this point, as on others ; but, in þÿHeaven sname, let the eminent men who are placed at the bead of the English Government I iv aside p ttv jealousies and unjust mistrusts.

" l,< t us understand one another in good faith, like holiest men as ue are, und uot like thieves who desire to client each other. For peace will secure his dynasty, strengthen his throne, enrich his people, develop his country, and ennoble his lame. But as the people of Euiope aie not statisfied with their governments; as atrocious despotisms still flourish, and i evolutional v clubs still smoulder, it is contrary to Divine justice aud human experience to believe that wars will not break out, sooner or later, and it would be fatal to Napoleon to remain a passive spectator of the broil. It is quite probable that Napoleon may have touched upon this point in his conference with the German Princes, as he did in his communications with the Pope and the King of Naples, If lie did, and if these Princes have sense enough to act upon his advice, the final conflict m >y lie postponed indefinitely. But historical experience proves that hereditary sovereigns are rarely willing to relinquish peaceably that which they are educated to consider their own by divine right; it is, at least, improbable that these German Kings and Princes and Grand- Dukes will be self-sacrificing enough to avert the peril which menaces. They are bred to consider revolution their natural enemy, which

they are bound to crush out ; and in parts of Germany revolution means freedom of speech and the press, informal gatherings of individuþÿals any thing, iu fact, which the Prince þÿdon t like. When the hour comes for an nprising in Ger many similar to that which we are now witness ing in Italy, the Baden Conference will no more save the German Princes than þÿNapoleon lov- s ing messages to the Emperor Francis- Joseph at the time of the Crimean war saved Austria in Northern Italy.

The Minister of Public Instruction and Worship has addressed a circular to the Bishops on the subject of a society which has been established for the defence of the Pope at Lyons. The object of the society, as described in the circular, is to support the Holy Si c in all its rights, spiritual and temporal ; its rule of conduct is entire submission to the Chief of the Church, without ever going beyond what ho wills, but also without incurring the least delay or manifesting the least hesitation in the accomplishment of it ; its means are prayer, the publication and the circulation of the best works in favour of the Holy Apostolic See, and the raising of the subscriptions known under the uamo of þÿPeter P s ence. Finally, it corresponds with a commission of Cardinals and with General dc Latnorieiere. From the London Times , August 16. THE REVOLUTION IN SICILY. (from the times' correspondent.) Messina, July 30. Another phase of the quick revolving hjstory of the war for Italian unity and independence is over. 1 myself, who am on the spot, and by no means a sceptic either iu t lie cause of nationalities or in the genius of Gaiibaldi, think now and then that I am dreaming, so wonderful is the progress of this resurrection of a people. 1 can only compare it to the growth of the aloe, which for years drags on its existence humbly close the ground, and which sends up all at once from amid its straggling leaves a tall powerful stem, which hutsts into flower in a night, filling the air all around with its fragrance. When ship after ship, carrying from Palermo Neapolitan soldiers and war munitions, disappeared behind Cape Zaffarano, even those most full of faith sighed at the new struggle which seemed in store at Messina It was no more on the steep but open heights of Calatafimi, nor in the narrow barricaded streets of Palermo, that we could expect to meet the enemy, but under the hundred iron mouths of a stronglygarrisoned and well-provided fortress. The only man who smiled at our apprehensions was Garibaldi. "Let them go wherever they please ; if we meet them again in Sicily, so much the better ; we shall not have to go so far to seek for them.'' This was the refrain he opposed to our grumbling at his magnanimity, accompanying it with one of those irresistible smiles to which even his enemies must yield. Not two months have passed since, and that

formidable fortress of Messina looks at our legions in mournful despair, dumb and lifeless, with its embrasures apparently empty, and inspiring so little fear that even the most timid of the emigrant inhabitants of the town are beginning gradually to return. You would almost think the citadel deserted, and, wire it not for the transports which you can see crowding outside of it towaids the Straits, and busy embarking stores and troops, and the line of sentries along the Plana di Terrauuova, in front of the citadel, you would think that the Bourbon soldiery had left altogether. The illusion is heightened by the circumstance of the Neapolitans having adopted the tricolourcd flag. You recognize, indeed, the blue paddloboxes of your friends the Neapolitan steamers, which you watched sending shot aud shell into the good town of Palermo, but you miss the dirty white flag of the Bourbons by which you always distinguished them There they lie in peaceful fraternity with the Scylla, the Descartes, and the Vittorio Emmanuelle, sporting apparently the same Hag, as if the union of North and South Italy, so much desired and longed for, was indeed a reality. It is not a week ago that things were different, and that quite another denonnement seemed impending. As late as the 23d ult. a note was sent from the Governor of Messina, General Clary, to all the Consuls, requesting that the foreign men-of-war, as well as the, merchant vessels, should leave the harb or, and the foreign subjects he embarked, as it might be

necessary to use means of coeicion against the town in case an insurrection to"k place, or an attack was made from the outside. It being Monday and mail-day for Naples the note was sent to the representatives at Naples The next day a formal order arrived in return from Naples, not only to dedst from all means of coercion, but even to evacuate the town, and, if necessary, all the forts Willi the order came a severe reprimand to General Clary, informing him that he had served his Government very ill, as, on the representations of the British Consul, Mr. Richards, Mr. Elliott at Naples had taken up the matter energetically, thus placing the Neapolitan Government in an awkward position. General Clary himself divulged this circumstance, complaining as he did of those to whom he owed, as he supposed, the reprimand from Naples ; and, no doubt, the

s T ". CROIX, A V I, C . | position of a Neapolitan General at this moment is not very enviable, lie is expected to make head against the current, but not allowed to use the means which had bent inculcated on him as the only efficient ones in such a case. He has been taught to consider bombardment as the only panacea against revolution, and now he is told that the Constitutional Government of Naples has a horror of such remedies. In order to give his soldiers a zest for fighting, he had encouraged their plundering disposition; and now he is told that constitutional soldiets are used for protecting, instead of destroying property. He had been taught to con.-ider the tiicolor as a horror, and the patriots of Italy as the greatest reprobates on the face of the earth ; and now lie is made to fight under this self-same banner, and sees his Government treating for the friendship and protection of the archfiend Victor Emmanuel. The moment the information spread through j the town that the foreign vessels had to leave the harbour, and that the foreign subjects were I to embark, a general panic seized the few inhabitants who still remained, and every one hastened to go off, either on hoard ship or to the country. The soldiers, seeing this puttie, | amused themselves by sending random shots about, increasing not a little the confusion. The Austrian Consul, who was making off' like the rest, was stopped by the soldiery, and when, in spite of his protestations in the name of his Government, he was detained, lie took

to running, and while jumping a wall received a bullet through his hat. A lady who was trying to make her way to the Marina received a hu let through her ctinoline while turning into a cross-street. The Austiian Consul was told iu answer to his complaint that the soldiers | could not be kept in order. The arrival of the National army on this side of the Straits has communicated the Italian fever to Calabria; while the Neapolitans still ruled supreme iu this part, aud we were far off, there was a good deal of talk of mov, menis iu Calabria, hut very little or not lung more. Nevertheless, the secret committees which had been j in formation for some time past in Calabria, as well as in every other part of the Neapolitan kingdom, began to show considerable activity. Prior to Garibaldi's landing and wonderful progress iu Sic ily, the eyes of Calabria were turned towards Naples. The programme was to upset the actual state of things, but very little union exi-tod as to what was to he done alter. As in Sicily, so in Calalqia Garibaldi's deeds, and the idea which guided these deeds, have placed before people for the first lime a j positive solution. A united Italy offered all those guarantees of internal freedom and development which had been until then sought for iu vain. Adopting the principle of union, thete was no longer any necessity lor trusting Royal oaths, so often broken, or invoking foreign protection, so continually used for selfish purposes. There were 11,000,000 Italians living already

under the constitutional system which all the rest desired. To unite with this uucleus was one's capacity, by Garibaldi's success. every the egg of Columbus brought home to The thing was so simple and so natural that it worked its way fast enough. As soon as Garibaldi's arrival was heard of all the commit- ( tees of the towns of Calabria sent represeii- I tatives to Aspremonte, with full powers to I come to an understanding about a common course of action. The resolution taken was to send a deputation across to invite Garibaldi to do lor the rest of the Neapolitan kingdom what lie had done for Sicily. The deputation arrived yesterday, and this morning, when Garibaldi returned home from his inspection at the Faro, 40 influential men, representing all the towns of Calabria, were waiting for him in the anteroom. However glad to see them, lie asked them to wait, for ho had first another duty and pleasure in store fur him. It was to welcome his old companions of the first Marsala expedition, who had arrived yesterday with the column from Catania, of which they form almost exclusively the corps of officers. It was the second time I have seen Garibaldi deeply moved daring the exciting success of his Sicilian career. The first time was when the prisomrs of the citadel of Palermo, surrounded by their families, came to thank him for their delivery. He had lost his natural

eloquence then, and was speechless as yesterday ; but on the other occasion he tried to conceal his emotion as a weakness, while this time he sremed to indulge in it with pleasure, tyu looked up again and again, letting his eyes wauder round the well-known faces who had answered his call, full of faith and without hesitation, and ca A them down again, as if renrembeting some one missing in the line, who was mouldering on the slopes of Calatafimi or under the ruins of Palermo At last, giving one long look of love to ail from those deep eyes of his, so toll of soul, lie told tlicm : þÿ My old faithful companions! The sight of you moves uie and deptives me of all power of expressing the joy 1 feel at your sight." Then, pausing fur a moment, lie repeated this, as several of the following phrases: þÿ " You were lew, and you have done much, and we shall be many to do what little remains to he done. There at e some of the first expedition who are not officers, and who, consequently, are not among you; greet them on my behalf, and tell them that with 111,11 like my companions of the first expedition no deeds are impossible. Many, many greetings to them.'' This reception h, ing over, it was the turn of tile Cal ihrese deputation, who, iu the name of the towns of Calabria, formally invited Garibaldi to come over, expre-siug the readiness of the people to toll w liim, ami asking for arms. Gai ibaldi told them how glad he was to see another member of i lie great Italian family rally

round the common banner to make one great and strong Italy, independent of the foreigner, and free turn the opptessor. He promised to come soon and si nd over arms before his airival. The unanimous dc rnnnd of the deputation was tin 'when.' A smile was the answer, followed by the word "soon," which elicited a < licer all around. Iu the evening 1 went to see our outposts towards the fort. They occupy a line in front of the houses towards the P una di TYrrnouova. Opposite to tin 111, at a distance of not more than 100 yards, is the Neapolitan lilt . drawn across the Piana di Terrnituova itsilf. You would scarcely believe tin- two lines hostile to each other, so much 1 bailing and laughing is going 011 between the two. According to the convention concluded by Medici, the officers and non-eomniissioiied officers can come with their sidearnis into the town; the soldiers only unatmed. During the first days ynu saw a gootl number of both about, taking off the tilings which they had been obliged to leave behind in the lint ry of evai-uation N, w thereare seaice'y any about, the it ason being, probably, the desertions for which the.-e promenades through the town gave opportuni y. August 1. This forenoon the armistice concluded by Medici was to end or to he prolonged. General Clary wished for an iuterwiev with Garibaldi himself, which was consented to, stud held iu the Casa Fiorciitioo, win re the first interview between Clary and Medici had been held. This interview was held in the greatest secrecy,

the only point made public h, ing the evacuation of Syracuse and Agosta. But this is only the least inipoitaut part of the transaction, for you must know we have come to this point that we care hut little about a couple ot fortresses with 200 guus between tin m, or evcti the total evacuation of Sicily. We fly at higher game ; and yet this unheard-of suec ss doi s by no means blind Garibaldi, who even at this moment is ready to listen to any arrangement, provided the gieat aim which he has placed before him he secuted. In the inerview of today Garibaldi laid down for the first time the conditions under which he would consent to stop iu his cnrcer of victory. A prolongation of the armistice for five days was agreed upon , and General Clary leaves this evening for Naples to carry there the conditions, lie is to be hack on the evening of the 5th inst. As for the conditions, their aim is to unite the north and south of Italy for all practical purposes, without actually driving away the Bourbons. It is one of those enthusiastic ideas which only Garibaldi can conceive, and which I am afraid mankind arc too perverse to carty out. The question is neither more nor less than of a kingly brothei hood, the assiniihitiuu of their two kingdoms, one policy and one attr.y. Of course in this union Victor Emmanuel, as the eldest of the two in the path of Italian in-

dependence and freedom, is to have the command of the whole army and the lead in the Italian policy to be pursued; Naples, in one word, to follow, and to he assimilated to Italy, retaining, however, its reigning family. As a first step in this assimilation an exchange of troops þÿ Italian troops to Naples and the Neatransformation, politans to the and north, to undergo a healthy thus become national troops. The navy 'idem.' The Constitution adapted to that, iu force in Upper Italy. The Customhouse line between the two portions of Italy abolished. These are the chief points of the conditions laid down by Garibaldi, and if they are accepted and carried into effect the power for evil of the Bourbons of Naples is broken. In the meantime the preparations are going on as it no j result was expected from these negotiations; indeed, the conditions are hard enough for us to ; be prepared lor a refusal. Yet, with most of the provinces of the continent ready to revolt, with the capital on the brink of a revolution, with a portion of the army not to be trusted, it is not probable that the proposals will he altogether refused. They will possibly be taken with advantage of to try direct negotiations until Piedmont, which have b.en unsuccessful now.

But t lis sick man was thought to have a new lease of his life, and we all began to put ourselves iu the position of End Eldon, who at last excused himself from giving advice on the subject of Turkey, because lie bad assisted at five successive salvations of that Empire, each time with a worse icsult. The youngest of us lias now seen the salvation of Turkey once, and the neec-sity of a second salvation is already imminent. Yes, Lord Stratford aud bis Eastern correspondents assure us that something very energetic must he done, the most stringent measures compatible with the law of nations must he had recourse to, or that country will perish. F,w people have had more practice in the precise use of language than this prince ol diplomatists, and it is impossible to suppose, that be could be blind to the natural lorce ot these terms. What is a " country ?" What is it to "peri.-li ?" What is the consummation we are once tnore invited to avert by terrible sacrifices? Are we all paralyzed with terror lest that fair creation of conque-t and diplomacy, the dominion of the Sultan, should vanish away

among those things which the poets tell us, and memory tells us too, are the fairest and the fleetest ? Lord Stratford himself is true to the traditions of dice. It is natural in him to wish to preserve the Turkish Empire, for should it fall the favourite work of his life would be undone. But we must frankly own that wo feel somewhat more tree to act like men and Christians now than we could do five years ago. That ill-starred war, those half-million of British, French, and Russian men left in the Crimea, those two hundred millions of money wasted in the worst of all ways, have discharged to the la-t iota all the debt ol Christian Europe to Turkey. Grant that, having for many generations patronized her, assisted her, advised her, and taken her iuto our confidence, we were bound to stand by her in the hour of her adversity, we then did our was very so utmost an for effort aud are quits. Never great her, made for so worthless an object, but it was made and is done. When the fighting was over we fought hard iu the Council for her; we we gave her money, for wc guaranteed her debt; advised, we pressed reforms, we urged the employment of the good men to be found even iu Turkey. All is over. In tbe course of five years Turkey has forgotten every warning, and exhibits betself at this moment as the worst governed country in the world, with the exception of China aud the kingdom of Dahomey. \Ve might now just as well hold conferences, prepare armaments, and vote millions to preserve on his throne tbe
man who celebrates tbe death of his father by digging a deep trench and filling it with the blood of some thousand human sacrifices, as for

just made for the puui.-hment of the Syrian atrocities would have given Turkey the option j Massacre ot' the Innocents, having been now reol herself repressing disorder and r -establishing peace by the means at her own command. This done, he is then for urging, and, indeed, j ago. It it is necessary to preserve the tradition compelling, upon Turkey the most vigorous and thorough reforms. One in in, who had himself massacred ' four hundred Christians h it in his care, was rewarded by the Turkish Government with a p st where he could repeat that service. \\ hat, then, is the Turkish Government now doing to clear itself from a crime which it finds is too great even for the toleration of Europe ? It may possibly attempt to 8 itisty us with illusory executions ; hut the arch offender, the man who is deepest, in the villany þÿ Kiuschid Pasha, when last heard of, was on his way to Constantinople rather as a triumphant hero than as a ci iminal. Old insults and invidious distinctions are revived, and even enforced by authority, contrary to the laws of toleration. Some exceedingly interesting experiments took place on Tuesday evening, the 31st, off Osborne-house, the beautrful marine tesideuce of her Mujesty, in the Isle of Wight, and also in Cowes-roads, with Professor þÿWay e s lectric light, and which wc believe are preliminary to more important experiments about to be carried out by the Government. The principle of the light is simply the application of electricity to a column or running stream of þÿquicksilver in this instance as fiuo as the point of a þÿlady s needle. So long as the voltaic battery retains power to act with its wires upon this column so long must the light þÿburn the strongest and purest light in the known world, and the nearest approach to sunlight that the skill of the chymistaud man ot science have yet produced, and this without actual combustion taking place or tire quantity of tire mercury beiug reduced, tire supply of acids to tiro battery being its sole expense after its first cost, excepting wear and tear. The professor with his apparatus left Portsmouth harbour in a steamer shortly before dark on Tuesday evening, and steered direct for Cowes. On the spottson of tho steamer was placed the battery. Abaft the foremast bung one of tho proþÿfessor simple s apparatuses as a mast-head light. On a movcablo circular platform placed on tho þÿvessel s after-hatch a similar apparatus to the one hung up aloft stood, to which was attached a lens, but. both of them as yet unlit. The apparatus is of the simplest possible form, consist-

ing mer ely of an oval-shaped pair of tubes connected at each end, a round hollow globe about, the size of an orange, in which is placed the mercury. The mercury runs from a point to a cup in tiro centre, enclosed within a glass tube, .and here the subtle liquid is heated lo a white heat, as it flows in a fine stream from the upper ball into the cup, and thence into the lower one, thus producing an indestructible wick. The wires which connect tire butt ry -with the apparatus were made by Me.-srs. Silver, and are, perhaps, tire most perfect of their kind yet con structed. These wires are coated with silver, enclosed in Indiarubber, and have an outside coating of hraid hemp, the whole pliable as common packthread. To look m the light, with a view to a close inspection of the cup, with the naked eye, would bo about as useless ns to look at the sun at noonday. A pair of coloured glasses, however, show that tl is light, which can only be compan d to the sun for its brilliancy and power, is only ol the same circumference as the clip its, f þÿ the size of a threepenny silver piece, and of little more diameter. Midway between tire aftermost light and the. voltaic bat fery is a brass standard a few inches high, with which the wires are connect, d, and by pressing a button on tire top of this, simple as the key rr a piano, the light can be given in flashes of as long or as short adulation as tire operatorpleascs. This is, however, more beautifully andcorrectlv carried out by a small instrument of Mr. þÿWay s

It consists of a pi ce of clockwork, having in front a revolving disc, the face of wl.iclr is covered with numerous holes with pins to lit in as may be required. In front of the disc are two small cylinders wrtlr pi-tons and arms attached As tho disc revolves the pins in its face lilt tire pistons in the cylinders and cut off lire connexion between lire battery and the lighting apparatus, producing flashes of light of any duration that may he required, with their accompanying intervals of darkness, and admirably adapted for a revolving light, or as a code of signals for night service. In f.ct, there would appear to be no limit to the us s to which this discovery may b« applied, and so simple is it in iis manipulation i hat the choicest music of the great masters may be henceforth accompanied by expressive flashes of electric light. When the steamer arrived off the Motlrci bank the light aloft was lit by at. taclring to it the ends of the wins front the voltaic battery. So soon as the glass tube became sufficiently heated to throw off the mercury from its surface the light exhibited its power and beauty, the þÿsteamer usual s masthead light, which was hoisted in its usual position, appearing but a dull red speck alongside it Its effect upon the human countenance was, however, by no means favourable, casting on all on board the steamer a strange unearthly hue. Mauve eo" lour, as it has become fashionable to term it on the þÿladies dresses or burnt els, was brought out by the light with great brilliancy. On reaching

Cowes-roads, crowded with yachts, and all displaying lights, the contrast between the electric light and those shown by the yachts was something wonderful. The electric light was shining in its pale pure brilliancy aloft, while the hun' dreds of lights displayed by the yachts and by the town of Cowes, its club-house and hotels, dwindled down to dull red specks. The lens applied to the after light threw broad pathways of light to and fro as the 1, ns might he directed, bathing the low black bulls of the craft that were in the line of light with a flood of sunshine as also the delicate tracery of their spars and r'Rff'ng A hut which left the steamer here for one of the yachts was lighted on its way by the lens. On the þÿsteamer s return Norris Castle was passed, and the light thowu on its picturesque

front. Ivy-covered towers, walls, and parapets were illustrated as with a stroke from an enþÿchanter wand. s Off Osborne-house the steamer was stopped for some time, and the light must have shown itself with good effect on the stil' waters of the Solent, in front of the beautiful marine residence of Her Majesty. The experiments, which, as already stated, are only preliminary to more important ones, were considered to have been fully satisfactory. With a light on this principle under her bows the Great Eastern herself might have lighted her path across the waters of the Atlantic.

SandPillaus. þÿ I have often witnessed a phenomenon on these sandy plains of Central Asia, which accounts, in some measure, for the innumerable sandy mounds that tire found in some regions. 'When seen tit a distance for the first time, it made a strong impression on my mind. About twenty pillars were in view, wheeling round .and licking up the sand. As they passed along, a cloud of dust was raised on the ground, apparently tight or ten yards in diameter. This gradually assumed the form of a column, that continued to increase in height and diameter as it moved over the plain, appearing like a mighty serpent rearing his head aloft, and twisting his huge hotly inti) contortions in his efforts 1o ascend. The pillars were of various sizes, some twenty and thirty feet high, others fifty, sixty, and one hundred feet, and some ascended to near two hundred feet. As the whirlwinds began gathering up the dust, one might have fancied that antediluvian monsters were rising into life and activity. The smaller ones seemed to trip it lightly over the plain, bending their bodies in graceful curves as llicy passed each other; while those of larger dimensions revolved with gravity, swelling out their trunks as they moved onward, till the sandy fabric suddenly dissolved, forming a great mound, and creating a cloud of dust that was swept over the desert. þÿ From Arþÿkinson þÿ s Travels in the þÿAmoor.

Singular Anecdote þÿ It is recorded | of the Marshal Luxembourg, that he took his mistress to the house of a celebrated Parisian artist, in order that she might see the likeness ot the marshal and sit tor her own. When, however, she saw the portrait, she declared that she had never seen any person like it. The marshal knew that this was mere prejudice, and persuaded her to go once ag ain to the þÿpainter h s ouse alter the last sitting, assuring her that it she should not then he perfectly satisfied, lie would cease his importunities. He had contrived, with the assistance of the painter, to thrust his own face through a canvas hung where the picture had before been placed ; but she, on perceiving it, persisted in asserting that it was no more like than before. Upon this the marshal could not keep his countenance, hut, by laughing aloud, discovered at once his stratagem and her obstinacy. þÿ A ales and Queries.

He was evidently in had humor, for, as lie emerged from amongst the trees into more open ground, 1 observed him madly charging anything and everything that he encountered, such as hushes, stones, &c. Even the whitened skulls and skeletons of his own species, lying scattered about on the ground, were attacked with inconceivable fury. I was much amused at his eccentric pastime; hut, owing to the openness of the

ground, and the quantity of the limestone there-abouts, which made objects more distinct, he was not easy of approach. However, after divesting myself of my shoes and all the more conspicuous parts ol my dress, 1 managed to crawl þÿ pushing my gun before me þÿ to within a short distance of the snorting beast. As lie was advancing in a direct line towards me, 1 did not like to fire, because one has little chance of killing the rhinoceros when in that position. Having approached to within a few feet of me, Ins attention was attracted, and suddenly uttering one of those strange þÿ þÿblowing noises, so peculiar to the beast when alarmed or enraged, he prepared to treat me in a similar manner to the stones and skulls lie had just so unceremoniously tossed about. Not a moment was to be lost ; and, in self-defence, I tired at his head. I shall never forget the confusion ol the animal on receiving the contents ot my gun. Ancient Pyramid in California. þÿ Another of those numerous evidences of a civilised antiquity in the New World has just turned up, it seems, in shape ot a great stone pyramid, composed op courses from eighteen inches to nearly three feet in thickness and five to eight feet in length. It has a level top of more than fifty feet square, though it is said to lie evident from t lie remains that it was once completed! This pyramid differs in some respects from the Egyptian pyramids, being more slender or pointed, and the outer surface of the blocks cut to an angle, that gave to the structure, when new and complete, a smooth or regular surface from top to bottom. From the present level of the sands there are fifty-two distinct layers of stone that will average at least two feet ; this gives its present height one hundred and four feet, so that before the top was displaced it must have been at least twenty feet higher than at present. How far it extends beneath the surface of the sands i t is impossible to determine without great labor. þÿ Literary Ga zette. TO HI. When I despatched my þÿSaturday letter s the Council was still sitting, and did not break up until half-past 7 þÿo clock. At its termination 1 ascertained that no resolution had been come to with regard to the Ministerial programme, and it was not until Sunday morning that it was accepted, nor until later in the day that it was published. Before I venture to make any observations on it, let me give it you entire, þÿ þÿ Programme of the Ministry. þÿ Citizens, þÿ When it was proclaimed by the Minister of the Inteiinr that a programme of the political tendencies of the Government would be published, it was the unanimous expression ot the councillors of the Crown þÿ a programme to which the Ministry do not now propose to create any further delay at a moment when the nation is piepaiing to send its representatives to the first Parliament. It is necessary that the country should know the general j laws by which the Stale is guided þÿ the principle in which the Government intends to trust at present for the settlement of the future ; that it should see the first steps of our national existence free and independent. In such a way public opinion, illuminated by acts and intentions, will proceed to the exercise of the electoral right with calm confidence iu the firmness of the new order of things, and with a conscientious deliberation in the choice of deputies. þÿ One of the first cares of the Ministry, con-

vinced, as it is, that there can be no national prosperity which is not based upon the infallible principles of morality and religion, will be that of protecting with vigour the worship of our forefathers þÿ the grand, solemn, imperishable expression of that Gospel which first proclaimed the brotherhood of men, the emancipation of the people. As to the interior, the full and sincere execution of the Constitution of 1848, and the strong and legal repression of every effort to the contrary, will form the unchangeable substratum of the Government. In 1 the salutary exercise of rights and duties there consecrated will be found the political regeneration ol the country, which reasonably waits to see vital, active virtue transfused into all aud every part of the organization of the Government þÿ an object to which the Government will pay regard. To begin with the cardinal reforms of legislative principles, the Government is preparing for the consideration of Parliament projects on various branches of public interest, and especially the foundation in the communes of a new life, more in harmony with political institutions; to introduce a better arranged administration, and while giviug relief to thoso classes really in want to assist in the umeliora- i lion of their moral sentiments, while withdrawing them from idleness and dishonesty ; to urge on the execution of public works with as much energy as the stale of the provincial and national funds will permit, and by simple and rapid

methods to liberate public instruction from the bonds by which it is restrained, and to render it in the. highest sense the þÿ þÿeducator, corresponding to the new life of the citizen, and coin- , mon to every social condition ; to establish thy forms of a happier progress of all material interests which on one side tend to the restoration of the finances by methods more useful to the State and less oppressive to the nation, and, on the other, to promote as much as possible commerce, industry, grand enter pri.-es þÿ especially railways, sources of these immense advantages of which all are sensible. Pa-sing on to secondary ameliorations which enter into the executive powers of Government, it. will carry t hi m out with prompt and deliberate resolution. Iu the judicious and good choice of public officers the Government has assumed, and will hold, as a rule, in giving public employment, the necessity of talent and the Well-proved merits of eitizens, certain that where they reside will be found Jove of justice, rectitude, and regulated liberty þÿ never a neglect of the duties due to the constitutional regime. To these propositions the Government calls the patriotism of all honourable men to assist them, and reminds them of the words of a great Italian.

ses of the electors to elicit from the national j representation the legal opinion of the real majority, to which alone it is confided to dissipate all uncertainty, to destroy even the importunate echoes of the past, and cause itself to be the guide of just and legal aspirations. þÿ SPINELMI. þÿ GIACOMO DI MARTINO. þÿ FRANC. LANZELLI þÿ It has been objected by some that the above programme is indefinite, but a statement of principles renders it impossible to enter into details. It is objected by others that it is nothing but words; but words must precede acts, and the future alone can prove if the latter will be born of the former. For myself, 1 am persuaded of the honesty ol the Ministers, and of their incieasittg power over the King, though events are marching on so rapidly that in all probability they and their programme will be swept away. As to some of the details, all the ! cuuutiy knows 1 that great changes have been made iu the þÿpersonnel of the Administration, and that the construction of þÿ þÿrailways is under the serious consideration of the Government. A demand was made for the removal of the Queeu-Motlier, but there appears no reason to doubt that her health is in a very feeble state, and the certificate of the medical adviser of the Palace, Dr. Rutnaglia, states that her removal is not at present possible þÿ indeed, she is to he brought up to Portici for the benefit of the ad-

vice of the physician of the capital, li is a step to be regretted, and will create great suspicion, but, nevertheless, is au undeniable fact Eleven ot the Camarilla have been removed at last, aud their places have been tilled by persons in whom the Government places confidence. His Majesty will not disband the foreign troops, as he deems them necessary to his deli nee iu ease of an attack from Garibaldi; and that this is probable and near at hand there is every reason to expect. I have beeu informed by a high authority that the auswer of the Dictator to Victor þÿEmmanuel letter s was to the effect that he did not believe it emanated front His Majesty . but from Count Cavour, aud that therefore he should burry ou bis landing on the continent A high official authority tells me also that, in answer to the remoustrances and declarations of the Piedmontese Government that it would not answer for the consequences of the contemplated movement, Garibaldi replied that he was too far compromised to draw back. Letters from officers in the army at Messina, dated the 28th of July, say that they were expecting to cross over daily, and, indeed, all the preparations indicate that the step will be shortly taken. The Neapolitan have concentrated a force in the Calabrias of near 40,000 men, and the Garibaldians expect some sharp work beefore they get up to Naples, but, unless the lloyal troops conduct themselves better than they have hitherto

done, it will be, I think, a short affair and a triumphal march. There is. to be sure, a considerable reaction iu the provinces, but it will be more likely to manifest itself after the fact, and I fully expect that the settlement will be uo settlement at all.

Garibaldi effected a landing in Calabria on the 12th August, and by the latest accounts had arrived at Montdeone. All appears to bo now up with the King of Naples. Part of the Royal Troops have fraternized with the insurgents. The King intends to try the i-sue of arms, and then withdraw to Gaeta His Ministers have tendered their resignations, but their acceptance has been declined. Austria will confine herself to repelling any attack which may eventually he made upon Vetictia. France will protect Rome alone, as the army of General Latnoricicre suffices for the defence of the Pontifical provinces. Piedmont is on the point of throwing off the mask and proceed to the annexation of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies within the biiefcst possible delay. The Count of Syracuse, uncle to the present letter to his nephew : Kiug of Naples, Ins þÿ addressed the following þÿ Sire, þÿ If my voice was one day rai.-ed and not listened to, to conjure the dangers which menace our house, may it now, while it predicts greater misfortunes, find its way to your heart, tind not be repelled by imprudent and more fatal advice ! þÿ The change that lias taken place in th condition of Italy, and the feeling of national unity, which has grown into a giant, during the few months which followed the fall of þÿI aleuno, have deprived your þÿMajesty Government s of the vigour necessary to rule a State, and ren-

dered a league with Piedmout impossible. The people of Upper Italy, bonified at the intelligence of the cruelties committed in Sicily, repelled in their hearts the Ambassadors Irotn Naples, and we have therefore been abandoned to the chances of war alone, without alliance, and exposed to the resentment of the multitude which has risen from all parts of Italy to the cry of extermination hurled against our House, which has become the mark for universal reprobation. M amvhile, civil war, which is already spreading over the provinces of the Continent, will carry away the dynasty into that ultimate ruin which the iniquitous arts of perverse advisers have long been preparing for the descendants of Charles III. of Bourbon ; the blood of the citizens, uselessly spilt, will again flood the thousand towns of the kingdom, and you, once the hope and love of the people, will be regarded with horror as the sole cause ol a fratiicidal war. þÿ Sire, while it is yet time, save our House from the curses of all Italy! Follow the noble example of our Royal kinswoman of Parma, who, on the breaking out of civil war, released her subjects from their allegiance, and left them to he arbiters of their owu destinies. Europe and your subjects will take your sublime sacrifice iuto account, aud you, Sire, will bo able to raise your brow in confidence up to God. who will reward the magnanimous act of your Majesty. Your heart, tempered by adversity, will become accessible to the noble aspirations

of patriotism, and you will bless the day when you generously sacrificed yourself for the greatness of Italy. þÿ With these words, Sire, I fulfil the sacred duty which my experience imposes upon me, and I pray to God that He may enlighten you, and render you deserving of llis blessings. þÿ Your þÿMajesty affectionate s uncle, þÿ LEOPOLD, Count of Syracuse. þÿ Naples, Aug. þÿ24. The punishment of the murderers of Christian men, women, and children in Syria has commenced. On the morning of the, 20th August, 1G7 persons implicated in the late massacres were publicly executed. Fifty-seven of the condemned were hanged in the most populous parts of the city, and 110 of the local police were shot in the square Djeuk Medan

These executions have struck terror into the inhabitants of the city, which remained tranquil. Those condemned to hard labour and detention will he taken, under a strong escort, to Beyrout, where they will be immediately embarked for Constantinople. Among the persons hanged were brothers, sons, and parents of the first men in the country. No attention was paid to their rank or dignity. From China we learn that the Biitish forces were ready for attack, but the French had protested against commencing hostilities, on account of having lost all their harness in the vessel which was wrecked at Amoy, and having also 2,000 men less than tbe British. TO Til E EDITOR OF THE WEST INDIAN. Sir, þÿ Yesterday a poor woman came to the þÿMagistrates Office, stating that she had lost her son and that she believed that he was ou board an Emigrant Ship bouud lor Demerara, called the þÿ Flora þÿMacdonald. On her affidavit, the Magistrates at once granted to a Warrant to was Police to proceed on board see if her Son the there; they returned with the boy, stating that there wi re plenty of children on board, crying for their mothers and wishing to return on shore; one child managed to get into the Police Boat, hut was immediately taken on hoard agaiu by the Crew, liie Police returned and stated these circumstances to the sitting Magistrates, who said they were unable to interfere. Upon the Inspector-General hearing this, lie immediately went to His Excellency the Governor who was sitting at the Town-Hall, and who at once promptly gave his orders for the Inspector-General to proceed on hoard to ascertain the truth, s, tiding at the same time for Mr. Cummins and asking him what he knew of the matter. Mr. Cummins corroborated the Inspector þÿGeneral s statement and at once with tin Inspector General, Mr. 1 nice M igistratc Gill, and three Police officers proceed on hoard the Flora Macdonald. On lb deck tl\erc were some twenty-two young children under the age of fourteen, some not being more than eleven and itirec not more than | four years oid (hut they were accompanied by their mothers). On questioning each of these boys and one girl not more than 13 years, nine

of them stated that they h id been inveigled on board and that they wished to return; ten hoys, two women, and the woman with her three children did not wish to return, also a white man. One of the consequences of the recent drought has been to give increased life to Emigration ; and so far as this offered relief to our superabundant population, by introducing them to a new field for their labour, instead of looking upon it with jealousy, it was regarded with favor, and every facility afforded for its operation, tint it is a system that requires to be watched very closely, as it is open to great abuses. An instance of this is brought to our notice by a Correspondent, þÿ( Anti-Slavery, who ) states that a vessel, the þÿ( Flora þÿMacdonald, ) was iibout to sail yesterday for Santa Cruz, with 22 children on board under 14 years of age, one half of whom had been inveigled away from their homes, anti were found by the Inspector-General of Police and Magistrates in great distress þÿ þÿ crying for their þÿmothers. We believe the ease is under investigation by the Magistrates, it being a grave offence to kidnap children and take them to a foreign Colony, where the conditions of service are very different from what obtains in Her þÿMajesty s dominions. In Santa Cruz slavery has been abolished; and þÿaltho in the neighbourhood of the Spanish Colonies where it is still maintained, we do not think there is any chance of Immigrants from this Island being carried to them ; at any rate we cannot believe such a crime would he countenanced by a respectable man like the Agent Mr. Bryan, through whom the children on board the þÿ Flora

þÿMacdonald were forwarded to Santa Cruz ; whose letter to show how satisfied with their condition in Santa Cruz were the Emigrants engaged by him and sent from this Island, we published in the last West Indian.

From the London Times, August 31. KOSSUTH IN ITALY. ( From a Correspondent.) Blllagio, Lago di Como, Aug. 2(5. þÿReuter s telegram has doubtless ere tins informed you of the unexpected arrival of Kossuth at this place. He came in by the steamer yesterday afternoon, at half-past 4 þÿo clock, front Coiico, and took up his abode at the Hotel de la Grande Bretagne, on the shore of the lake, midway between Coiico and Como. At halt-past 7 þÿo clock the hotel and the adjacent gardens were illuminated, and bonfires were also lighted on the shore, which were quickly responded to by a number of similar beacons at several points along the long mountain ranges of the opposite side of the lake. The population of Bellagio is hut small; yet scarcely an inhabitant could have been

absent from the spot when the Hungarian liberator had taken up his abode. The enthusiasm of the people was very great, and at each discharge of cannon their cries þÿof Viva Italia!" þÿ Viva Unghtria!" þÿ Viva Francia!" and though last, not leasl, þÿ Viva Inghilterra!" were as loud and noisy as the most vehement patriots could desire. The town band, consisting of nearly 40 musicians, assembled under the window of the hotel, and played several airs with much precision, the most popular of which seemed to he the Hungarian March; after the performance of which Kossuth appeared at a window, and bowed several times to the populace, which act was the signal for renewed vociferation. At about 10 þÿo clockthe crowd dispersed, and the lights of the hotel were slowly extinguished. By a singular coincidence Prince Albrecht of Prussia arrived from Coiico by the same steamboat in which Kossuth had embarked, and proceeded at once to his elegant villa opposite to Bellagio, from which he had been absent for two years at Candana. Saturday was also the birthday of the son of the Marquis þÿd Azeglio, in compliment to whom many ofllie villas were brilliantly illuminated along the shores ofthe lake, the effects of which, under a lovely Italian sky, with a bright-shining moon, were most fairy-like. At an early hour this morning the town hand took a boat, and as they approached the Hotel de la Grande Bretagne serenaded Kossuth, who again appeared and acknowledged the compliment offered to him. The

movements of this remarkable man are at present unknown, hut the general impression here appears to he that he is about to take some part in the war of liberation, than which nothing ran he more popular in this part of Italy, if the signs of enthusiasm every where apparent may he taken as genuine. The hatred against Austria, at all events, is most unmistakable. The Princess l)emidoff is staying at the Hotel Genazzini, which is adjacent to þÿKossuth shotel. The fair Russian seemed to he much interested at þÿKossuth s reception, and as soon as the serenade of this morning began appeared on the belvedere of the hotel.

FRANCE (FROM THE þÿTIMES CORRESPONDENT.) Paris, Thursday, 7 a.m. You will perhaps have already seen in the A ord ot the 29lh inst. the following ominous paragraph, with which that paper, supposed to derive its inspirations t r o m Russian chancelleries, commences its political summary : þÿ þÿ The Italian question daily tends more and more to become the pivot ot the situation ; it is more serious than is generally supposed, and it would he strangely to deceive oneself to imagine that it is limited to the dynastic affairs of Naples, and even to the eventualities of an attack by Garibaldi on Venetia. We said a faw days ago that the Italian movement symbolizes in some sort the secret struggle that is going on between the past and the future, between the old policy, which will not yield its place, and a policy more in accordance with the ideas and necessities of our epoch. Must one he astonished after that, if on tile solution that movement shall receive certain alliances, and consequently peace or war, depend? It may be said, then, without exaggeration, that the Gordian knot of the situation is there. In a month we shall know if that knot is to he untied or þÿcut. þÿ Ibid.

Threatened Eombardment of Vera Cruz. Veka Cuuz, Wednesday, Aug. 8, 1860. I understand that the United States steamer Pocahontas will, at the request of Mr. Elgee, Charge þÿd Affaires of the United States leave to-morrow at 8 a. til. for Pensacola, bearing important dispatches to our Government at Washington, and I avail myself of the politeness of a friend to forward you a few interesting particulars þÿ so far as now known to the þÿpublic of a fresh complication (within a few days) between the Government of Juarez and the SpanishComimrdore þÿ an event, I deem it to be, full of pressing present and future importance. Your readers will remember that, about the time þÿMarin filibustering s expedition (fitted out at Havana under the auspices of the Spanish Government and authorities of the Island of (Juba) was expected to appear at Alvarado, which place was to have been declared a port of entry by the Miramon faction, should that expedition have proved suec ssful, but which port had been previously declared closed by the Juarez Government, a bark, the Maria Concepcion, under Spanish colors, belonging to þÿMarin s expedition, with a valuable cargo i f warlike munitions, appeared in the neighbourhood of Alvarado. Of course, so soon as the Government here became acquainted with such fact, one of their small war-steamers was sent to Alvarado with orders to capture the bark. This was done ; the vessel was brought to Vera Cruz, and the officers and crew were imprisoned. Within a short pul'd the Isabel- Catolica þÿ a

very fine Spanish side-wheel frigate built in England þÿ arrived at the anchorage off Sacrifictos from II i vatu. A large screw-frigate and brig-ol-war had been there for some time pteviously. The Spanish Commodoie immediately proceeded to business, inloiming the Juarez Government that lie had come with instructions to demand : First, the n lease of the imprisoned ctew of the Spanish bark captured at Alvarado ; second, the surrender of the vessel and her cargo; third indemnification for ho b the list and s, cond propositions ; and, fourth, hoisting of the Spanish flag upon the Castle of San Juan þÿd Ulloa, with a salute of twenty-one guns. Tweuty-J'our hours only were granted yield to compliance with these demands of the Spanish Govcrumeut þÿ through their Commodore; and, in the event of a refusal on the part of the Juarez Government, a bombardment w..s piomised ; and, fuither, accompanied by the threat that tin hark would be taken from under the guns of the Castle, where she was anchored. This war-message, produced, a- might uatutally have been expected, much consternation among the merchants, foreign residents and officials of Vera Cruz. The Government of Juarez immediately sent to the Spanish Commodore, by the Captain of the Port, a temperate and dignified, yet firm response to these demands First, that the crew of the captured bark had long since been released from imprisonment; second, that the vessel aud her cargo would not be surrendered, because both were in

the proper Courts for adjudication, in accordance with the laws of the country, and that their final decision had not been rendered ; third, should the Courts decide that the vessel aud cargo were illegally captured, then they would be surrendered, or the Government would hold itself liable for such indemnification as was both legal and just, and that the fourth proposition could not at present, be entertained. Preparations were accordingly made, and every precaution taken by the Government of Juarez to relist, in the most determined manner, and to the list extremity, the tlnoatem d bombardment of the Spanish Commodore. Troops and ammunition were in constant movement throughout all t lie night aud day of the 3rd and 4th Inst., and I am of the opinion, from reliable information, as well as from my own observation, that the Spanish war-vessels would have received a most effectual and impressive lesson, had their threat bcou carried into execution. I am now thoroughly conviuced, aftei mature reflection, that this movement ou the part of the

S T. C R 0 I X A V l| S , Spanish Government is but the basis of future interference between the Government of Juarez and the Miramon faction. It is full of pregnancy, and, no doubt, will be the more pointed by next November, when Miramou is again expected before Vera Cruz, to attempt a second time, its reduction. Then, 1 have not the slightest doubt, that the Spanish Government will avail itself of the presence of Miramon to press their present demand, and upon the smallest quibble, bombard Vera Cruz fiom the sea-side! There are abundant evidences here that they intend to make some decided movement in favor of, and to assist openly, the Miramon faction ; and it remains to bo seeu whether our Government will allow this to be done by any European Power. If the Government a of the United States docs not interfere in very prompt and firm way, then it is the impression of intelligent aud well-informed persons here, that the Juarez Government must fall, and result in the establishment of Spanish influence over Mexico! Shall this be allowed ! How to prevent such an unhappy consummation 1 leave it to far wiser heads than miue to suggest and direct. But I must here remark that the refusal of Congress to place at the disposal of the President of the United States the necessary means to successfully meet aud overthrow these constantly recurring acts of European Governments with the þÿufi airs of Mexico, lias been the source of all this trouble. Now, should the Spanish Commodore bombard Vera Cruz, 1 much fear a very savage revenge.

Already threats have gone forth that, shall an event, every Spaniard iu the country in such be assassiuated, and it will certainly render it extremely hazardous for any foreign residents to he out of their houses, day or night, during a I bombardment, because the populace cannot distinguish, intelligently, between a Spaniard and done Europeans of other nations. Can nothing un- be to resell'1 t his rich and beautiful, hut happy country from its present terrible conflicts of passions, scenes of blood, and violences ot every description ? An unusual and exceedingly severe gale of wind occurred hero on the night of the 31st ultimo. 1 hear from s "ine of the officers of the United States frigate Savannah, Hag-ship of the Home Squadron, that she came very near being wrecked. She was anchored under þÿ Green þÿlslaud at the commencement of the gale, as was also the United States steamer Pocahontas. The heaviest winds were from the westward of noi th, occasionally, and suddenly veering to the N. E., whilst, the tremendous seas came from the eastward. The Pocahontas got up steam, and being well under the reef, was comparatively secure. The Savannah was less fortunate; she dragged her two anchors, and befote a third could be let go, she was so faraway from under the lee of the islands and reefs as to have no prottclion whatever, þÿ got into the troughs of fhe heavy seas, and rolled so heavily for four or five hours, that at times it was thought impossible for her to withstand the tremendous

surging. The seas came aboard, sweeping her spar-deck and washing away two of her hoofs from the port forward davits Her hatches had to he battened dowD to prevent her from swamping ; and for many hours she was, besidi s, in the greatest danger ot going ashore ou the north reefs of Saciificios Island. She dragged, before being brought up by a third alichoi þÿ port i þÿsheet down opposite to Sacrifich s I should judge from all accounts that there must have been a considerable current setting along past the reefs towards the s mthward and eastward ; otherwise the Savannah must have gone aslioie and proved a total loss iu such a sea She lost, also, her starboard sheet-anchor and 1 GO fathoms of chain ; hut these have since been recovered through the exertions of her Master, Mr. Fitch, with the assistance of the United States tm timer Pocahontas. It was after this anchor was let go and lost that the port sheetanchor was cast, which, providentially, brought her up. I am told that it was such a night as her oldest officers and men never before experienced. 'The Savannah is now at anchor under Sacrificioa, repairing damages. The U. S. steamer Pocahontas and stoic-ship supply are also anchored near the flag ship. The officers and crews of the several United States vessels continue healthy. Those on board the Savannah are cotuplotely wearied out

with their unnecessarily prolonged stay in this debilitating climate, and greatly need a change. They are anxiously looking for the Brooklyn, with þÿ home orders. The Brooklyn went to Pensacola the early part of last month with Minister McLane It can hardly ho contemplated by the Navy Department to keep the Savannah's crew upon police duty at Vera Cruz, after their already long and arduous services upon this coast, þÿ particularly when their two years have expired. A small French brig-of-war, the Mercure, is also at Sacrificios. The city of Vera Cruz continues healthy þÿ the recent heavy rains having greatly contributed to its healthiness, by washing away some ol the accumulated filth of months. It is now tolerably decent. There is no news of importance from the interior. Miramon is reported to be at Guanajuato, without means of any kind, and awaiting funds. All the small towns in the vicinity of the city of Mexico are reported to bo in the hands of the Liberals. A ennduda, with $2,000,000, is on its way from Mexico to Vera Cruz. Col. John T. Pickett, U. S. Consul at Vera Crux, goes to the United States iu the Pocahontas. It was currently reported to-day that the Government of Juarez had decided to give up tlie Maria Concepcion, but I cannot trace it to any official source. If they should pursue such a course, it would settle the whole question be tween the two Governments. I do not believe that the Juarez Government will do anything of the kiud. A few days since it was asserted that the

British Charge d' Affaires, Mr. Mathews, was at þÿMiramon camp, s endeavoring to patch up a peace, by compromise, and thus bring Comonfort again into power. This country is not yet ready for anything of the kind: it requires an honest military chieftain, with abundance of talents, and a full military chest. Nothing short of it.

The tort was attacked on the morning of the (itli inst , at daylight. Three of Gen. þÿWalker s men were slightly wounded. Fifteen of the enemy were reported killed, and a number wounded. The main body rapidly followed up this advantage, and after half an þÿhour shard fighting, drove tho em my from the fort.
