He also took sixteen cannon þÿ among them one twenty-four pounder and a brass twelve pounder which cominauds the þÿPass one, hundred and twenty-five stand of aims, eighteen hundred pounds of powder, and a large quantity of munitions, including clothing, pi ovisions, etc. Gen. Walker feels confident ol being able to hold Truxillo for the next four mouths against any force that can bo brought against him. lie is assisted by Gen. Cabanas who is opposed to tho present President, Gen. Guardiola. The latter has applied to Gen. Carrera, Dictator of Guatemala, for assist ance, which has been refused A large number of the natives are joining Gen. þÿWalker standard. s The schooner þÿ Clifton was not seized by the
authorities at Belize ; but her batches were forcibly broken open, aud in consequence she was abandoned under protest of her commander

Captain McCormick. The þÿ þÿClifton had n regular clearance from this port, and her ot cargo was not contraband at Ruatan, the place her destination. Several masters and merchants have frequently carried arms and ammunition from this port and Belize to leu .'an, under regular entry, after paying duties. Below we give Gen. þÿWalker pi s oclamation to the people of Honduras. To llte People of Honduras : More than five years ago I, with others, was invited to the Republic of Nicaragua, and was promised certain rights and privileges on the condition of certain set vices reudeied the state. We performed the services required of us ; but the existing authorities of Honduras joined a combination to drive us front Central America. In the course of events, the people of the Bay Islands find tin tnselvos in nearly the same position the Americans held in Nicaragua in November, 1855. The same policy which led Uuurdiola to make war on ns will induce him to drive the people of the Islands from Honduras. A knowledge of this fact lias led certain residents of the Islands to call on the adopted citizens of Nicaragua for aid in the maintenance of their rights of person and property. But no sooner had a few adopted citizens of Nicaragua answered this call of the residents the the Islands, by repairing to Ruatan, than of acting authorities of Honduras, alarmed for their safety, put obstacles in the way of carrying out the treaty of the 28th of November, 1859. Guardiola delays to receive the Islands, because

of the presence of a few men be Las injured; aud thus, for party purposes, not only jeopards the territorial interests ol Honduras, but thwarts, for the moment, a cuidiual object of Central American policy. The people of the Bay Islands can be engrafted ou your - lie public ouly by wise concessions properly made. The existing authorities of Honduras have, by their past acts, given proof that they would not make the requisite concessions. The same policy which Guardiola pursued towards the naturalized Nicaraguans prevents him from pursuing the only course by which Honduras can expect to hold the lslunds. It becomes therefore a common object with the naturalized Nicaraguans, and with the people of the Bay Islands, to place in the government ot Honduras those who will yield the rights lawfully required in the two States. Thus the Nicaraguans will secure a return to their adopted country, and the Bay Islanders will obtain full guarantees from the sovereignty under which they are to he placed by the treaty of the 28th November, 1859. To obtain, however, the object at which we aim, we do not make war against the people of Honduras, but only against a Government which stands in the way of the interests, not ouly of Honduras, but of all Central America. The people of Honduras may therefore rely on all the protection they may require for their rights, both of person aud property. Wm. Walker. Truxillo, Aug. 7, I860

GEN. WALKER IN HONDURAS The ex-President of Nicaragua is certainly a wonderful man. He holds on to an idea with a j tin act v which is very up' to live out the spasmodic or languid opposition of his adversaries. Calmly calculating, but for is ever on the watch brilliantly inventive, lie a chance to elude official vigilance, aud tor an opportunity of giving expression, in some practical lorni, to his theories and his hopes. The pitcher that goes too often to the well is sure to get broken ! The cunningest lox at last leaves his skin at the þÿbatter s shop. But it is also true, that perseverance often achieves success and consummates the most desperate enterprises. Which ot these truths is to be illustrated in the career of General Walker, it is for time to determine. At the present, moment, public curiosity is strongly aroused concerning an ment, and is combined with his latest move- interest which none can help feeling in one who lias manifested so much of bolduess, energy and resolution. Mingled with these sentiments there is, too, in the South, a geueral sympathy with þÿWalker s designs. Whatever faults may have been charged to him, whatever of error he may have committed, it is believed that, had success have tended his earlier efforts, the effect would at bceu felt in an extension of Southern influence and an aggrandizement of Southern power. However silent he may be as to all other subjects, as to the character of his immediate plans, or of the means by which he expects to consummate them, he never lias hesitated to avow

that the welfare of the South and the spread of Southern institutions held a conspicuous place iu his programme. All this has very naturally tended to stimulate Southern hopes lor his success, and to excite Southern regrets for his failures. The movement towards Honduras does not, at first sight, seem to paitakc of the character to which wo have referred. Nevertheless, those who know General Walker, who arc aware of the persistency with which all his actions are made subservient to an original purpose, will readily believe that his present course has, at least in his mind, a logical connection with his previous efforts. When he left this city for Ruatan, it was supposed that lie went to that island, by invitation of its inhabitants for the purpose of assistiug them to uiaintaiu the independence of the Bay Islands against the llondurean Government. At the same time, it was thought that he intended to make Ruatan a base of operations for a further movement in the direction of Nicaragua þÿ a land which is known to be the ultima, thule of his hopes and aspirations. There is nothing in the intelligence just received to weaken the latter supposition. Indeed, from the language of the proclamation published iu and that Walker the Delta of last eveuiug, it seems his companions assume still to j that his mission to Ruatan But be citizens of Nicaragua. had lor its object to it does not appear 1 establish the independence of the Bay Islands. On the contrary his statements lead to the in-

ference that lie went thither for the purpose of securing t he retransfer ol those was islands to not duras. liut in this matter be acting, Hon- as the agent of the existing Houdurcan Government, but as the auxiliary of a revolutionary party. This explanation gives the key to the present movement, aud renders intelligible wliat before was obscure. There are complications in the politics of Honduras, as well as in the politics of the other Central American States. Of course we can not attempt to unravel those complications ; nor is it necessary to do so. It is enough to state that tho party now in power is headed by General Guardiola, the actual President, and that the party out of power is headed by General Cabanas. The party outof power takes the usual means employed iu Central America þÿ a pronunciamitnto , an appeal to arms, and a call tor help wherever it can be found. In this contest tho Bay Islands play an important part. Some time since a treaty was concluded between England and Hunduraa, under which the Islands were to be restored by tho former power to the latter.

But the inhabitants of the Islands, who had enjoyed a kind of semi-independence, wished jtbe transfer, anti its acceptance to bo accompanied with certain guarantees which the Government of General Guardiola was unwilling to grant. Thereupon the islanders made arrangements with General Walker to come to their assistance for the purpose of enforcing their demands, supposing, of cout se, that the transfer would take place on the appointed day. The effect of this arrangement was thwarted by the refusal of Guardiola to accept the transfer, and by the consi quout presence of a British force which remained on the islands at the request of the Hondurean authorities. In the meantime, General Oabansu, an ex-President of Honduras, aud the leader of the opposition party, took up the cause of the islanders, and made the maintenance of their local rights and privileges a portion of his programme of revolution against Guardiola. Of course this was done to secure the co-operation of Walker, who had returned to Central America, as the champion of the Bay Islands in their anticipated struggle with of Honduras. Walker counts ou the aid a large party in Thus Honduras, in carrying out his designs. It is stated that General Cabanas had actually joined him, and that many of the natives of the country had enlisted under his standard. Of course, as matters now stand, nobody ean interfere with him. He professes to be merely acting on behalf of the Bay Islanders, and in the interest of the Cabanas party þÿ not in order to

prevent the annexation of the Bay Islands to Honduras, but iu order to accomplish that purpose. Thus he is not interfering to violate the treaty with England, but, at the request of one of the parties in the State, to cause it to be carried into effect. This fact alone gives him a great advantage over Guardiola, who has refused to accept the Islands, instead of taking immediate possession of them, in the name of Honduras. It is highly probable that the Cabanas party will succeed in the contest, and that the Islands will be annexed to Honduras, under tire guarantees they require. But what is to come then remains to be seen. þÿ Ibid.

E XTRACT OF THE PROCEEDINGS OF THE BUR- GHER COUNCIL OF ST. CROIX. Monday the i7lh Sept. 1860 the Burgher Council held an extraordinary meeting as fixed at the last adjournment of the Council. Absent were Mr. Rothe on a mission for the Council and Mr. R. Knight, the latter having left for Europe. The following cases were referred. Government acknowledges the preliminary communication of the Council on the subject of Coolie-importation, and expects further proposals, especially for the terms of subscription, on which planters desirous to employ Coolies may have them imported ; also forwards a copy of a memorial from several planters declaring themselves desirous to obtain 380 Coolies. þÿ The whole tf this matter having been reported on, the Council, considering the extent of risk and of outlay in question, the small number for which subscriptions have been ottered, the difficulty of arranging effective securities, and also that some immigration of laborers has taken place and may be expected to continue, resolved : 1, That it is not expedient, that any further steps be taken by the Council in order to obtain an importation of East India Coolies. 2, That there be granted front the landtreasury to such planters, as shall before the end of the year 1863 import East India Coolies under contracts for not less than five years, a bonus of thirty dollars for each able individual landed. 3, That all other expenses or pecuniary responsibilities arising from any such importation do not concern or come to the

charge of the Landtreasnry. 4, That Government, in conformity with the above, be requested to take over any further negotiations and arrangements, which might eventually be occasioned by any scheme for importing Coolies. Government communicates, that it being anticipated, that several matters of importance will shortly be laid before the Council, and considering that Chamberlain Rothe has been absent for more than 2 months, and that Mr. R. G. Knight has left the island, the Council is requested to have the two vacant seats filled by newT elections. Letter from Mr. R. G. Knight resigning his seat. þÿ The sheriffs to be requested to cause new elections. Government communicates, that delay has been granted until the 1st of October for payment of taxes 1859 ; it will be arranged, that levies be effected according to laws before the end of October. From the Loudon Times, Sept. 14, 1860. CENTRAL IT A UY. (FltOM THE þÿTIMES CORRESPONDENT.) From Naples 1 have fresh news of considerable importance. The check Garibaldi met. with at Santa Maria and Cajazzo had to a great extent sobered his judgment. Addresses to him as well as to King Victor Emmanuel had been sent round for signatures at Naples and in the provinces, and had been covered with the names of the most honourable persons in the country. The municipal corporation of Naph s vied with private citizens in their eagerness to convey to the Dictator the wishes of their countrymou, and an address was equally circulated among the national guard, of which their Comlnamler-in-Chii f. General Don Mariano þÿd Ayala, it would he difficult to know t lie reason why7, forbade the publication. The scope and tenour of all these manifestoes are one and the same. They recalled the Dictator to his former purposes and declarations ; they reminded him how he was bound in honour and loyalty to King Victor Emmanuel and Ids dynasty ; they besought him to put no further delay to the annexation of the Two Sicilies to the North-Italiati necessity kingdom; finally, they urged upon him þÿ of reforming his Administration or the rather, rendering his Administration at all pos sible þÿ by abolishing that Secretary-Generalship which constituted a State within the State, anti deprived the Ministers both of all real power and constitutional tcspon.-ihility. This was a palpable hit against the S> cretary-Gi m i ni, Dr Bertani, who, having set the police to tenet out

the supposed promoters ot the addresses, obtained Irom tlie Dictator a summons of live conspicuous gi litlemen to appear before him at Caserta. tt was, under gentle forms, a positive order of arrest, as Major Htagnetto, of the þÿStall , was sent to the live persons in question, conveying to them the Dictator's desire that, they should proceed to Caserta under his escort. The. prisoners were Silvio Spaventa, Bellelli, Scia hiya, Pisanelli, and þÿD Afflitto, the three last named members of the late Administration, and Bellelli lately appointed þÿ1 ostmaster-genoral and Director of the Telegraphs and Railways. Ga ribaldi, who knew nothing of the proceedings adopted against these gentlemen, glanced at the numerous signatures under the address which lay before him, and, as lie did not see any of their names, he concluded there must be some mistake, and was bowing them out, when Spaventa boldly avowed that he had signed the address and highly approved it. Whereupon a long and bitter alteication arose between the General and bis piisoiier. Garibaldi made use of the most intemperate language. He did not hesitate to characterize all those who followed the policy of Favour as a pack of either fools or knaves, either led into error by their own imbecility or sold to power by the baseness of their souls. Favour, Farini, Fanti, and tlm majority of the Italian Parliament o«me in for their ample share of his withering abuse. He then turned against the Emperor Napoleon, a man despised by him even more than hated. Ho

declared that lie, Garibaldi, was at this moment lar stronger than the French antociat; that the latter had þÿ la coda di þÿpaglia (it is a pet phrase of his. and ho used it repeatedly in his interview with Tommasi and Piria at Ebo' 0 þÿ þÿ Napoleon had a straw tail, and lie was the man to set lire to þÿit. He then proceeded to vindicate his own conduct in the past, and his views and designs for the future. He would not hear of annexation till ho could bring the whole of Italy uuder one standard, and he would wage war agaiust all her foreign foes to the last drop of his blood. He kuew he was made the butt of a thousand calumnies. Among other charges brought against him was this oue, that he allowed himself to be intiuenced by the persons about him, and especially domineered by Bertani. He launched into long eulogies o(

þÿBertani devotion s to him, of his great abilities, of bis unwearied activity and aptitude for business ; but he rejected the idea of any of the measures he bad adopted having been suggested, much less forced upon him, by Bertani. He consulted his own brain and heart, and took counsel from no other man ; nevertheless, ami this was the vital point, he had resolved upon parting with Bertani. lie expected him in a few moments and would lose no time in bidding him renounce his Secretary-Generalship and remove altogether from Naples. $ @ 1 o j 1 A\ v I: $ THE þÿPOPE S PROTEST On the subject of the recent entrance of the Piedmontese into the States of the Holy See the Cardinal Secretary of State has addressed the following note to all the members of the 1 diplomatic body residing in Rome. from the Vatican, J8tb inst : þÿ . It is dated þÿ The uudersigned greatly regrets the necessity of communicating to the representatives of the foreign Powers to the Holy See, a statement of facts more and more deplorable; but the force of circumstances is so grave, and the impetuosity of the violence used towards the most pacific of Sovereigns, the august Head of the Church, is so astounding, that ho canuot refrain from addressing to them the present communication, being impelled thereto not only by his duty as a Minister, hut also by the express counnaudsof his Holiness. þÿ SinceI had the honour of explaining to your Excellencies by the note of the 12th ist. that the Piedmontese Government was taking j bos ile measures against the Government of the Holy See, without, any provocation on the part of the latter, adding crime to crime, adding armed revolt to its legitimate authority, in order to obtain possession of the provinces which remain to the Holy See after the usurpation of theRomagnas, the Pontifical Government, relying on its right, has made and is still making every possible-effort, despite the small number of its troops, to arrest the impetuosity ot the invasion ; but the þÿenemy s forces are so overwhelming that it is not possible the defence can

hold out long. Pesaro having been captured the Piedmontese took prisoner the Pontifical Delegate, who was even exposed to outrage, as also the commandant, who had resisted the att o k. On the other hand, a numerous body attacked Peiugia, which, after repulsing a vigorous assault, was compelled to surrender, and the Genera! in command, with tin- whole ganison, became prisoners of war. The same corps then marched upon Foligno and came to Spoleto. Orvieto lias been carried by volunteers, partisans of Piedmont, who now threaten Viierbo. 11 The Holy Father has seen nearly all the States which are the patrimony of the Church and of catholics torn away from him hit by hit, not withstanding that, the Emperor of the French has declared to Piedmont that he should have opposed the recent invasion that bioken oil' all relations with and would have Government, if the latter had not given him the assurance that the noted intimation made to the Holy See would not ho carried out and that the Saidiuiuus would not attack the Pontifical troops. þÿ In this state of things the undersigned Cardinal complains and protests, in the name of his Holiness, against acts so destructive of all laws human and divine, and as assailing the independence of the Supreme Head of the church and the integrity of the temporal domain, with wit ch he has been invested by the dispensations ot Providence, for the good of religion and of the Church, and which the Church has lawfully possessed for so many ceuturies past.

þÿ therefore I request your Excellency to communicate to your august Sovereign this complaint and protest. The principles of justice, order, and morality, which all princes are bound to maintain and defend for the safety ot their thrones, give assurance that they will oppose a harrier to this spirit of usurpation, which, treading all law under foot, spreads disorder, by armed force, in other States, in order to consummate spoliations to the injury ol the lawful sovereign. What also gives no less confidence to the Holy Father is the thought that attention will ho paid to the prayers of so many millions of Catholics scattered through all kingdoms, who earnestly implore that a term may be put to the anguish and calamities in which the common father ol all has been plunged. þÿ The undersigned assures your Excellency of his high consideration, &c., þÿ þÿANTONELLI.

wards we marched off to meet the enemy, preceded by General de Lamoriciere. Wo were of the brave þÿPimodan division. s The battle commenced furiously, and would have been much more severe but for the cowardice and treachery of an Italian regiment, who passed over to the enemy, and by whose hands it is generally believed General Pitnodau fell mortally wounded; the Swiss ran away, and left me alone with only 30 men to fight against a whole regiment of Sardinians. What could I do but retreat? þÿ which I effected by getting into Loretto. After 24 þÿhours waiting in expectation of assistance, I was compelled to capitulate, and surrendered as prisoners of war. 'The Sardinians received mo and my gillant comrades with military respect, such ns dipping their colours, Ac. When the fight commenced we wore only 5.000 strong; there were against us 32,000 men, with ten batteries of English rifled cannon. The brave Lamoriciere was forced to dash through the enemy amid a shower of shell and grape, and succeeded in getting iuto Ancona. The garrison of Spoleto contained only 300 men, and my gallant countrymen held out as long as it was possible, aud inflicted severe punishment on the enemy. I am told that 600 Sardinians fell, besides several officers. Be so good as to write to my father at Boulogue, and tell him I am to march immediately with my men to Genoa, and thence proceed to þÿFrance.

þÿMAZZINI S MANIFESTO. The hide of Naples publishes in its number of the 24th of September a manifesto of Mazzini. It is beaded, þÿ Neither Apostates nor þÿRebels. The following are the concluding sentences of the manifesto : þÿ þÿ Wo claim the liberty of saying, not that a republic is the best form of Government, but that j we, 25,000,000 of Italiaus ought to be masters in our own country ; that we can he so if we all wish it ; that our liberty is there on the point of our bayonets and in the firm resolution of our souls ; that it is not in the counsels and acts of France and Chanceries. To make it dependent upon a whim of Louis Napoleon or any other man is to prostitute it, to risk losing it again, and to declare ourselves unworthy of it. þÿ Wo claim the liberty of saying that between the programme of Cavour and that of Garibaldi we prefer the latter ; that without Rome and Venice there is no Italy ; that, excepting the war of 1 85A, provoked by Austria, and maintained, at the price of Nice and Savoy, by the arms of the Emperor of the French ; excepting the invasion of the Roman provinces, provoked by us, by a necessity which we created, no initiative of Italian emancipation belongs to the programme of Cavour ; that Rome and Venice will remain slaves of the stranger if the insurrection and war of the Volunteers does not restore them to freedom þÿ We claim the liberty of saying that a free and united country will not be formed by annexing this or that province to Piedmont, but by amalgamating Piedmont and all the provinces

ot Italy, and Italy with Rome, which is its centre and heart; that the immediate annexation of the conquered provinces that have acquired liberty, by placing them under the programme of Cavour, and taking them away from, Garibaldi, stops the movement, takes away the strength of the country from the hands of him j who wishes to employ them well, to place them in the hands of a man who wishes to condemn them to inaction, and for a time to suppress the dominating patriotic idea. þÿ We claim this and nothing else. Refute but do not calumniate. Do not always sillily or wickedly repeat that we Work for a Republic, when for two years we have never spoken of a Republic. Do not obstinately judge us without reading us. l)o not repeat, blind servants of any Ministerial Gazette, affirmations a hundred times denied by facts. Do not excite against us, by perfidious falsehoods, the passions of a people who owe to us in a great measure what they feel and what they have achieved by unity. Falsehood is the base, weapon of vile cowardice. Belief without investigation is the wont of þÿidiots.

(From the Barbados West Indian, Sept. 25, 18(i0.) ANTIGUA. There has been quite a stir in our commercial circles during the past week or ten days, arising out of the discovery of what appears to have been, a deeply laid plan to defraud several merchants of the city, by two Foreigners, Louis Delmail, and Victor Gutlroy, his nephew, both of whom a few years ago became naturalised and settled down in the Island as Agriculturists, having become possessed of a small Sugar Lstate each. They were both regarded as honest, hard working men, and had attained reputations un successful Planters. The sudden departure and continued absence of Mr Gutlroy from the island (both Delmail and himself being largely mixed up in money and property transact io ,s) and the discovery that both parties had been systematically availing themselves of the extensive credit they possessed, by raising large sums, and turning all their possessions in money, besides dismantling their Estate of all the moveables, such as the Coppers, Stocks &c., together with the tact that Delmail was making preparations to leave the island, aroused general suspicion, when steps were taken to prevent the þÿlatter escape. s It would seem that Delmail, imposing upon the credulity of several merchants, had put abroad a report that a relative of his þÿWife in s France had died, bequeathing him a large amount of money and property, upon the strength of which, it is now found In' lias drawn Hills upon the House of Kothchilds, and another firm, to the extent of some .£3,500. Of

the fate of these Hills nothing can be known until the arrival of the coming and following Mails from Europe. Mr. Delmail, we learn, even to his intimate friends protests his innocence of any intended fraud, asserting that he had full power and authority to make the drafts in question and that they will be duly honored ; but when the antecedents of himself and connexions, now well known here þÿ all of whom were humble peasants of France þÿ are remembered, it appears more than likely that his alleged inheritance (if any) of ,£3000 will dwindle down to just so many Francs. .Such, at any rate, would appear to be the impression now of the majority of his Creditors, many of whom, we learn in utter despair, have accepted compromises of their claimsþÿ among them Mr. Thomas Thibou, at whose suit the delinquent was arrested. The whereabouts of Air. Delmail at the present moment is involved in considerable doubt þÿ it, being pretty general y believed that be has left the island. þÿ Tinas.

Some of the most valuable portions of our West India possessions have gone out of cultivation for want of labour, which is to be procured in any quantity from British India, from China, and from the Coast of Africa. The African labourer is best suited to the purpose of the West India Plante'-; but he cannot be obtained simply because an African immigration is liable to be abused or misinterpreted. Hut the other day it was announced that the King of Dahomey was about to destroy 2,000 human beings at one fell swoop, in obedience to some barbarous custom of the tribe he is said to govern ; and it has been stated that our cruisers have been ordered to that part of the African coast to prevent, if possible, such a revolting sacrifice of human life. Now, surely it would be possible to make some arrangement by which the African chief in question would consent to part with his subjects, who, if they were permitted a choice, would, we should say, prefer to cross the Atlantic under a contract with the white man, to being sacrificed to a horrible superstition of which they are the unhappy victims. What has been considered, and justly considered, a most salutary arrangement for the natives of British India and of China, could not work badly for the African. These are considerations which, we ventured to submit, are well worthy the attention of Her þÿMajesty s Government and of the British Parliament. African labour is of vital importance to our West Indian dependencies. It is going to waste on the shores of the

African continent. Worse than that that ! it has been, and it will continue to be, dissipated, in obedience to a hideous and revolting superstition. If this country is to interfere in the interests of humanity, let end to the suppression of savage rites, the interference be directed to a practical þÿ and the utilising of the human material which is annually consumed in maintaining them. A system of African immigration established under proper auspices on the West Coast, and governed by proper and stringent regulations, would, we have not the slightest doubt, answer this most desirable end, and before long we should hear that supplies of labour were as easily procured, for British or French account, and under a system which would afford a guarantee against abuse, in the Bight of Biafra as in the Hay of Hengal. þÿ Mitchells Maritime Register, Aug. 25.

Liberator of Southern Italy. Anonymous Writing. J a o There is no reason why a patriot should always Be a martyr. A very good and great divine, who has but just passed away front us, writes amusingly : þÿ I love liberty ; but hope it can be so managed that 1 may have soft beds, good dinners, tine linen, Ac., for the rest of my life. I am too old to fight or to þÿsutler. This was a very frank confession, but it is full of plain homely good sense. The more helps, therefore, we can find to protect such lovers of liberty in time of peril the better, or liberty may chance to keep few friends. Now an admirable device to preserve them in good heart is the right of anonymous writing. It is the principal point, indeed, in which our press differs from that of despotic countries. It is the very essence of a free and useful Press. It, permits men to write when they would fear to speak. Anonymous writing is a surer guarantee against injustice and oppression than any form of government could he. Even the most liberal and popular executive wields fearful instruments of quiet and insensible tyranny, which the victims of them can neither

escape nor resist, but which they may expose and bring to shame. Instances of harshness and iniquity every day occur, of which the law can take no cognizance, and which would have no chance of hearing or redress, were it not for that tribunal which is always open gratuitously and to every complainant. Neglected or unrewarded merit, which can obtain no audience from men in power ; long services which have been discarded or superseded to make way for the high-born and the favoured; sufferers under unjust and brutal exertions of undeniable power; þÿ till these can make their appeal to a judge whose authority is the greatest, and to a court whose publicity is the widest, in the realm. In Great Britain, scarcely any public or private iniquity can now be done in a corner. Silence can never he counted upon; secrecy | is never sate. The right of anonymous writing is a protection the value of which cannot he exaggerated. It is one that no power can silence, no money can corrupt, no iluttery can lull to sleep. To abolish it would be to bid the soldiers of truth go forth to attack the fortresses of error without armour, while any fool might launch poisoned arrows at them in security. To stand up for it stoutly, therefore, is not to encourage a nameless body of literary men in tt course of doubtful honour, but it is to protect life, to insure property, to fence the altar, to guard the throne, to give space and liberty to all the finer powers of man, anil lift him up to his right place in the

order of creation. In estimating the high tone and character ol the Press, the chief cause must never be forgotten which secures and maintains it. It is a good thing that the Press should j authorship. be exempt front all tho small vanities of Whatever influence a newspaper writer ntay wield, he generally remains unknown. The names even of the editors of journals which exercise the most important influence on public events, are scarcely heard beyond the circle of their own private friends. Year after year they toil on with unequalled ability, enetgy, and public spirit, yet iu complete obscurity. Connection with political literature among tation. The suppression of anonymous writing would undermine the healthful power of the Press more perhaps than any measure which could be devised, and would take from it a great guarantee of its earnestness and sincerity. We are already a great deal too much disposed to be swayed by authority rather than argument, to consider the man who says a thing more than the thing said. Unfortunately, the world is much too apt to be misled by presumption. It cannot understand that wrong is not right because it is sanctioned by power. From the London Times, Oct. 2, I860. CHINA. Although we talk much more in England about Rome and Naples than we do about the bay of Tah-lien-hwan, our intimate home sympathies jump most eagerly towards the last news from that far-away locality. Its uncouth name has hitherto found its way into no map, and its position is an impenetrable secret to the majority of those English families who know it only as the temporary abiding place of some one who is very dear to them ; hut a little boat accident at Tah-lien-hwan has much more English interest about it than if the whole Austrian navy went down in a storm in the Grand Canal at Venice, or after a collision with the unlighted Rialto, and the news of half-a-dozen cases of fever upon the sh res of that bay with an unmcmorable name would cause more real alarm in England than the m ws that malignant malaria had held its own at Rome against the approaching winter, and had seated itself triumphant upon all the seven hills. 1 he fact is, that our own kith and kin were, at the last accounts, away in that distant and unsung land, where there are neither priests, nor ruins, nor deadly miasmata; and upon this last point we are glad to be well assured. Nothing can be more satisfactory than the tidings our correspondent sends us of the condition of the expedition at the latest despatch. So far as regards health and comfort both forces were in the highest state of prosperity and efficiency. Of our own men less than four and a half per cent, were on the sick-li-t, and the majority of

these invalids were suffering from no more grave malady than that of cut feet the conse- þÿ quence of bathing upon a beach strewed with oystershell8. The 99th had but two men absent from duty, and of serious cases there were not more than one per cent. Nothing could be better than this Nor need friends at home be too anxious about the creature comforts of our j claim all absent warriors. While they pursued their games like Trojans on their way to Italy, abundant markets enabled them to satisfy the appetites the exercise had excited, and to eat like Trojans too. The French, with their usual promptitude in settling themselves with all the appearances of civilization about them, had huilt, a town with its Hotel de Ville, probably with its cafes and estaminels, and certainly with its surrounding villas and its They also were in good fellowship with their neighbourhood, and in the full enj ymeut of the sheep, goats, pigs, poultry, eggs, vegetables, and fruit which a Chinaman is always ready to bring out to an enemy who pays ready money. To these the British added a large demand for beef, and although John Chinaman always looks sorrowful at the untimely death of the labouring ox, even these wire led to sacrifice before the almighty dollar It the reader would put his finger upon the two spots where this highly satisfactory state of tilings was ill course of occurrence, he must search in his map of China for the Gulf of Picheli. lie will find the entrance to this Gulf narrowed by two pro-

montories, the northern ol which is marked þÿ þÿRegent s þÿSword. and the Southern þÿ Shanþÿ tung Promontory. þÿ On þÿRegent s Sword is the bay of Tah-lien-hwan, where the British station was, and on the Shantung Promontory, near where Tang-chow is marked upon the map, is the French station of Clie-fow. From these wtll-cliosen stations the two expeditions were to start at daybreak of the 26th of July, and to rendezvous on the other side of the Gulf. Long cro this our Armstrong guns

must have had their first opportunity of testing their efficiency in rivalry with the rifled cannon of the French, which have already done service in the plains of Lombardy. There is, however, a very considerable disproportion between these two allied expeditions. We have 26 gunboats for the fight which was to come off at the mouth of the Peiho ; the French had 6. We have 11,000 men; they have less than 5,000. We have 1,050 cavalry as superbly mounted as horsemen can be ; they have 4 Spahis and 4 Chasseurs þÿd Afrique. We have a fleet o! 200 vessels of war; they have 39. We have ti mounted batteries, two of 12-pounder Aimstrongs, and two ol 9-pounders ; they have three batteries of 4-pounders rifle bored up to 8. Moreover, we have efficient means of landing men, horses, and material; and so have they according to present arrangements, for they propose to show their brotherly affection by sharing ours. The landing arrangements were not very perfect, even at. Clie-fow, for when we paid them friendly visits at their home, Adurirals, Generals, and Ambassadors weie constrain- 60 ed to pass in undignified procession through yards of mud and surf pickaback, with are of brawny natives for holdfast. A\ o the tails about to return the compliment to our good allies at Peh-tang, and to take them in our boats to terra Jirma. The original plan, duly set forth in writing, had been that the French should land on the south of the Peilro, while we landed at Peh-tang on the north ; but after reconnais-

sance made the French found that they could not make sine of their landing, so they go with us. Jack grumbles a little at this arraugi inent ; for he complains that, after having waited for an assistance he does not want for more than a month, and after having lost the best of the fighting season, he now has to carry his 1 relicb friend ashore, where he will infallibly break the plan of attack, and make a run out orders, of and whip his tricolours out of his pockets, and the glory. Thc.-e little rivalries and jealousies always will happen in combined operations. Such unions seldom add much to the cordiality of the forces joined in them, and two still think it would have been wi.-er if the we expeditions had each gone its own way, each had, if that be the point intended, given and other rendi zvous at þÿl ekin However, the dogs arc now slipp. d, and our next letters will give us results. It we are not flourishing gardens, j successful this time, no fault will lie at the door of those who prepared the expedition. It. is at any rate pleasant to know that we have made some advance iu the ait of sending out a fleet and atniy. We have placed a powerful expedition on shore 16,000 miles from Woolwich without a disaster, and in as perfect a state of efficiency as if they were all congregated at. Mount Edgecumbe. After the first blow is struck promptitude and rapidity will bo everything, and there will be no more delay for anybody, not even, we will hope, for diplomatists, until enough has been done to render their

work easy. The plan, we believe, was to land the first division at Peh-tang, where it may be reasonably supposed that the Chinese, will not expect us. Peh-tang is the mouth of the unnavigublo river into which the Chinese attempted to lure Mr. Bruce. It is about ten miles north of the mouth of the Peiho. It is defended by two small forts, and if the river should have been found not to be staked the landing party would make a dash at these forts, and, having taken them, the whole land force would march across the neck of land which separates the Peh-tang from the Peiho river and thus obtain the rear of the Taku forts. When this march

of 12 miles had been effected, the gunhoats would cross the bar, and the forts be attacked at once from land and river. This plan may of course have been modified by circumstances, and it may have happened that the Peh-tang river might be found to be too formidable in its fortifications to be thus summarily dealt with ; but circumstances point out this as obviously the plan of the first intention, and, as two months have now elapsed since the attack must have been made, not even Russian telegraphs can render it. an indiscretion to mention it. Such is the crisis of our affairs in China as it stood on the 25tlr of July last, and as it has been more elaborately depicted by our correspondent who attends the expedition. For tidings of the i-sue we must still wait, and it is vexatious to feel that the want of telegraphic communication alone cone rals from us events of vast national concern which aie very possibly known to another liurop an Power.

(Continued from No. 80.) Anonymous Writing. Were nil writings signed, therefore, the public would devour with eagerness and curiosity the feeblest and most unsound reasoning of a man in office, but pass lightly over, or perhaps not read at all, the unanswerable logic of a writer unknown to fame. The public would lose also, or silence, many of their safest guides and best instructors. Many unsparing condemnations which ought to be expressed, many grave charges which ought to be brought forward, would be suppressed if the shelter of the anonymous were withdrawn. One of two risks would he incurred. Either things which ought to be said would remain þÿunsaid facts which ought to be dragged light would be hushed up and to concealed ; either the task of correcting delinquents, detecting jobs, and dealing out the fittest measure of refutation and of blame must be abnegated, or it must be left to literary bravos. A far higher and more conscientious class can now venture to undertake the functions of censors and denouncers than would be willing to wield

the lash, had they to do so without a mask- To say the harsh things which ought to he said, to make the fierce onslaught which needs to be made, to stigmatize the evil deeds which it is for the interests of the public should be ruthlessly exposed, is pleasant and easy only to the unfeeling and malignant. One of the most important services ren- j dered to the nation by anonymous writing consists in the exposure of abuses in the various departments of Government. These abuses are chiefly known and most thoroughly comprehended by officials. To I suppress the right of anonymous writing would be to close the mouths of such persons completely, as long as power, vanity, and jealousy remain inseparable. Nothing can be clearer, therefore, than the value and necessity of anonymous writing in this case. It enables a Government servant to make the same reply as was made by an engineer, who hud invented a of new Geneva. of ordnance, to the Government piece The magistrates, cowed by France, told him thiit he could not be permitted to fire republic. his piece and exhibit its powets in the þÿ that makes no sort of difference, tor þÿ Very þÿwell, said the man, þÿ I can very easily fire over the republic. Many instances occur in which statesmen and public functionaries may be highly blameable, without committing offences for which they may be impeached or punished by law. Moreover, no person can contend, with a grave face, that publicspirited men should institute impeachments, quencies by instead the of short exposing official means and efficient delin-

of the Press. An impeachment is a parliamentary proceeding, competent only to a majority of the House of Commons. To use no machinery for the abatement of any public nuisance, but one so cumbrous, would be indeed an agreeable arrangement for official wrong-doers. They might well feel secure in their places, and amuse themselves with the destruction of the country at their leisure, if they were never to hear the voice of censure till it was recorded in the votes of Parliament. Such an idea is absurd. Whoever thought ol telling a man who had beaten another in self-defence, that he ought to have submitted in the first instance, and then indicted for the battery, or brought an action for damages? A gentleman who so demeaned himself would be generally ridiculed and avoided. Such an argument was never even used in an answer to a case of verbal provocation. be But latitude may allowed to self-defence, in it is said, that some order to repress aggression or insult, and to prevent others from beginning an affray. The principle of anonymous writing may be defended on precisely the same ground. It gives to individuals a power of exposing and punishing offences which no other vengeance can reach, and which each individual has an interest in repressing. Assaults upon our liberties by bad rulers, injustice, malevolence, unprovoked outrages of superiors upon inferiors, and a thousand other evils of the same kind. An anonymous writer has no advantage over his opponent lie merely chooses a

field in which a powerful opponent can have no advantage over him þÿ a fair field and no favour. He may be as easily answered and refuted as il lie signed his name, and he will be heard always under protest. For his opponent to skulk and lie in ambush, therefore, to talk of anonymous writing, to abuse his adversary for choosing equal arms, is but one of the shifts and contrivances of conscious weakness and error. It is mere cowardly begging the question. What have names to do with facts and reasons.

T.. C A 0 I X AVIS , Members of Parliament, advocates at the bar, clergymen in the pulpit, are each protected by their respective privileges. They are not personally responsible in private for the expression of opinions which may affront men in power. Anonymous writing gives the same privilege to the author, nothing more. He enjoyes this privilege moreover, with a far higher claim to it; for as he derives neither personal honour nor repute from his labours, however successful, he is at least entitled to demand that he shall not be subjected to personal incon- Ven fence The private motives which may induce a man to write anonymously are as numerously and powerful as any which could influence a reasonable being. In early life, every author, not utterly blinded by vanity, must be conscious that Ins style is unformed, his thoughts immature, his arguments doubtful, his knowledge small. The mind has its youth as well as the body ; at.d something ought in fairness to be allowed it. The greatest intellects that have adorned the annals of mankind have not always shone steadily and early. Young men see clearly, but they do not see far enough They are so eager to remove a stumbling-block as not to perceive that the cumbrous mass is sometimes the keystone of a valuable arch. There is a Quixotry also about them which often leads them into needless hostilities. They seldom estimate quite correctly the strength of an adversary, or the degree of his culin the very best men there pability. They have not yet will learned be always that

something to condemn and something to pardon. But a young man need not think it shame to follow Milton, and covenant with his readers that for some few years, lie may go on trust with them. Wisdom is not raised from the heat of youth nor the vapours of wine, like the trifling jests which flow waste from the pens ot vulgar scribblers and trencher-loving parasites. Many weary years must pass in toil and vigils before the bright countenance of perfect truth appears at last through the quiet, and still air of delightful musings, and the seraphim come with the hallowed a fire þÿstudent altar to touch and purify of the thoughts. Nevertheless, circumstances or necessity may compel young a man to write, however poor an opinion he may have of his labours; and it is unjust to force on him in riper years, errors which he has long ago, perhaps, discovered, regretted, and outlived. It cannot be said that a man ought not to write till his mind is ripe. Some of the most delightful books in the language have been written by mere boys. Keats and Chatterton were still youths when they died. It would have been as hard to silence Pascal in his teens, as to oppose the rise of Pitt to power at a time when other men have hardly left off cricket; but it would be incredibly absurd to suppose that either wrote or thought as wisely in their youth as in their manhood. On the other hand, a man may alter his opinions, like Strafford, so that his first thoughts may be better than his last. It is tor the public to

judge these things. No man is obliged to adopt opinions merely because they have been written. Locke wrote anonymously because he feared to be engaged in personal quarrels, which would have prejudiced his arguments. Men will sometimes yield to correct reasoning when they will not to those I Gohah by whom it is employed. For rich men the advice of Johnson on this point was as plain and sensible as usual : þÿ If the authors who apply to me

have money, I bid them print boldly without a þÿname. þÿ þÿObserve, says Scott, in a letter about the þÿ Quarterly þÿlleview to Mr. Sharpe, þÿ carefully, this plan is altogether distinct from one which has been proposed by the veteran Cumberland, to which is annexed the extraordinary proposal that each contributor shall place his name before his article, a stipulation which must prove fatal to the undertaking. If 1 did not think this likely to be a well-managed business, 1 would not recommend it to your conþÿsideration. Again, he says, þÿ As strict secrecy would be observed, the diffidence of many might be þÿovercome. No man can be blamed for not choosing to be persecuted. A writer may begin to conceal his name from modesty, and continue to do so through prudence. There may not be danger in writing the truth to day, but there was yesterday, and there may be again to-morrow. It is never possible to calculate on the feelings of those in power. It is remarkable that Luther thought at first that his well-deserved censure of abuses in the Church would be received with favour by the pope. He was miserably deceived. Had Wickliffe written anonymously, perhaps he would not have been harried into a palsy for translating the Bible. The influence of fear has been constantly put forward with great insolence us the chief reason which induced writers to conceal their names. It has been very loudly asserted that there is something cowardly in anonymous writing; but this opinion

will appear, on examination, to be only one of those which the world has been content to receive without thought. It would not be courage that would induce a man alone and defenceless to expose himself voluntarily to a bund of armed fanatics, however the welfare of society might be interested in their suppression : an unreasoning fanaticism equal to their own might indeed urge him to do so, and so might rashness, madness, or despair. As for courage, what more can the people ask of their champions than that they should expose themselves to the risk of a long and s disheartening conflict with men in high places? it is risk they that though This impossible always incur; for an anonymous writer can be discovered, he is likely to be among the suspected, and the mere suspicion is enough to ruin his worldly fortunes. A man who attacks an abuse is like one who attempts to pull down an old house. If he succeeds in so gigantic an attempt, the ruins are certain to fall on his own head, and overwhelm him. The gain is to those who stood aloof. It is for the lookers-on to dance and make merry upon the site. It was surely courage enough in Sampson to fall beneath the ruins of the temple he overthrew There was no need for him to brave the stones of the Philistines, while he shook the pillars which supported it True courage consists in meeting fairly an equal enemy with equal weapons. David was is the champion of the chosen people. He supposed to have acted directly under divine guidance ;

but he did not offer to fight Goliah with a 1 club. He used a sling, which put him upon more equal terms with his adversary. The giant might have used a sling also; David could not m t club. There is no reason in the laws of honour or of war why David should have fought hand to hand with a stronger man than himself. had the best of his legs and his strength. He might easily have run away ; but if they were to fight, the pious hero determined it should be on even terms. (To be concluded.)

Anonymous Writing. (Concluded.) What opinion could be entertained of the prudence or discretion of any general who engaged his army in a battle where defeat was certain. þÿ We must þÿfight, said a thoughtless officer to a renowned commander in front of a superior enemy. þÿ That, answered one of the most valiant captains of a valiant age, þÿ (hat will be as l þÿplease. It is fortunate for society that anonymous writing enables the opponent of any powerful abuse to give a vu I gar bully, who charges down upon him with an army of furious sycophants, the very answer that was made by the great duke of Schomberg. It is very easy to tax a writer with cowardice because he refuses to commit an act which is tantamount to suicide. Cowþÿ ardice, however, is really on the other side, that worst, basest, and most revolting cowardice, which would award punishment to an honest adversary in an argument, because he cannot be refuted by reason. A fellow who challenges an anonymous writer to avow himself, gives but a small proof of courage. He only braves a single enemy when his blood is warm. The author may expose himself to a thousand. Some may fight, some might murder, some might calumniate, some might ruin him. A writer may well hesitate before laying himself open to the ignoble vengeance of those who, perhaps, could and would effectually silence him by starvation. A rascal who is a dead shot will not shrink from an encounter with a philosopher, who, perhaps, notoriously never fired a pistol in his life.

A scamp drunk with wine and rage cannot fairly claim credit for valour by threatening a man who may be obliged to allow himself to be bullied without resistance, who may be a bishop, or old, or blind, or onehanded. Again, a person in high authority, or his favourite, needs no courage to call a subordinate to account in the most offensive manner for any writing, however harmless, which may affront them. They will not fight : they fear no consequences ; they expect to be met on ground which gives them every advantage. No prudent writer will submit to this, and accept an adverse judgment. If he did so, lie might voluntarily allow a man in power, or his dependant, to blacken him for life by any verdict, no matter how unjust, passed upon any publication, or passage of a publication, no matter how innocent. He might voluntarily place himself under the ban of a sentence which, in the eyes of many thoughtless persons, would degrade both himself and his labours. Personal fear in such cases may be put altogether out of the question. Fear truly, but fear of a very different kind, may sway a writer. He may fear for the progress of a sound principle if subjected to the open condemnation of high authority. He ma/ not fear the day of judgment, but the day of no judgment. Nothing can be more different than personal and political fear. It is the flimsiest of artifices to confound them together. If a man really desire to serve his country, why should he take a step which would put it in the power of any bravo,

with a pistol or a bludgeon, to silence him for ever ? What is called the law of honour, is sometimes put in force by cunning people to enable them to practise very dishonourable arts. For instance, grave moralists and philosophers have reluctantly admit- 1 moner with a single punch. But how ted that duelling is sometimes justifiable,

s t « c B 0 I A V I S . and sometimes inevitable. Some of the most eminent men in the world have fought duels. Hut suppose a body of subtle and shameless rogues take advantage of this to push an empty- pated fellow forward, to offer a mortal insuft to a man whom they wish out of the way ; is that man to be blamed who sees through the j paltry trick and despises it; who contemptuously declines to enter on a deadly struggle with a fool, at worst merely the silly tool of þÿothers malice? Why should he become the dupe of so shallow an artifice ? A great rogue always puts a small one foremost. Is it necessary to the public welfare that a useful writer should be exposed to the deadly resentment of some of the most powerful and unscrupulous people in the country ? Appeals to cold iron are no better proofs of a þÿman s honesty, than hot iron and burning ploughshares were of female chastity. Any bully may acquire a cheap reputation for courage who challenges an anonymous writer, but what is the reputation worth ? It neither clears his character nor establishes his innocence. When there is no argument against a writer but a fist or a pistol, his position must be very strong indeed. An Anonymous writer is not entitled to shrink from an encounter of wits with his adversary ; but he may fairly say, You shall þÿ not break my head because it is not so thick as yours. You shall not bring into a discussion elements which do not belong to it. If you can reply to me, do so; but you shall not murder me if I can help it,

because I have the better of you in reasonþÿing. Assuming, however, that an anonymous political writer sometimes may feel personal tear, is it ill founded? The spirit of revenge is so universal, that no man can be known to censure an abuse with safety. Wise men will not write for a punishment of this kind. Had De Foe not written anonymously against the frightful excesses of the Mint and Friars, the lawless ruffians who foflnd sanctuary there would have torn his heart out in their rage. A savage fool, one Blaney, chivied Swift into a ditch on the strand, towards Howth. In 1702, John Tutchin wrote some able articles in the Obser valor. He was prosecuted, but set free. One night the unfortunate newswriter was waylaid by a gang of ruffians, and beaten so cruelly that he died of his wounds. A near relation of Lord Castlereagh openly expressed his wish to shoot Peter Finnerty, a writer in the Chronicle, who had commented in very just terms on the Walcheren expedition. A political writer may object to have his head punched, to be beaten with blud- | geons, or to be assassinated ; but is this a valid reason why his opinions should be j fallacious, and that the man who punches his head, or maims or murders him, is entitled to the honour of having refuted him? If a hard fist is to become the evidence of political truth, there will be joy at the Seven Dials, and in the purlieus of Whitechapel. The Billingsgate pet may strut with perfect confidence into the House of Lords, overturn the Chancellor, and rout the

bench of Bishops. If the fighting system had prevailed among our fathers, Molyneux might have been Premier. He might have entered public life with the utmost | assurance, and knocked down everybody who stood in his way. He might have answered every argument with a black I eye or a backhander. He might have broken Lord þÿChatham head s with his own crutches, and doubled up the great com-
would such a method of settling disputes

appear to sober people ? Who would have liked to see the difference between Locke and Filmer, or between Bently and Boyle, settled by a stand up scuflle with dictionaries? Perhaps there were many owners of rotton boroughs, fresh from the banks of the Cam and the Isis, who could have thrashed Karl Grey in three rounds. But this would not have proved that he was wrong in carrying the measure of parliamentary reform. There were certainly farmers in Yorkshire and Bucks, who would have settled the corn-law question bv a wrestle with Mr. Cobden in three minutes But the qualities which make a statesman do not necessarily make a prizefighter. A man may argue correctly, and be a weak hitter. Few scholars and statesmen would not shrink from this new tax upon eminence. It is possible to have wisdom without the fortitude to become a martyr. Many valuable men would not have firmness enough to meet beggary and blows as the meed of ennobling and anxious toil, or shame and wounds for honourable aspirings. But shall men, who may be as timid and as great as Lord Bacon, or John Locke, unnerved by the confinement which long studies ask, be scared from conferring their priceless benefits upon mankind by ruffians confident of the applause of society ? If so, unhappily their choice may be soon made, and improvement will march but slowly. To sum up, the fact of a man writing anonymously is certainly not a reproach to him in any sense that can be conceived, either as a gentleman of birth, honour, or

piety. Charles I. was an anonymous writer, and so was Louis XVI. All the great Tory statesmen and all great Whig statesmen, all the bishops and all the lawyers of repute, since the Revolution, have followed so excellent an example. Even the pious Mrs. Hannah More was an anonymous writer, and gave us her ideas upon marriage with greater freedom in consequence. Therefore, this tower of strength and bulwark of the liberties of the Press may be strenuously defended without a blush or a misgiving. It may be defended in the name of truth, us the most fearless and redoubtable opponent of error. It may be defended in the name of reason, as often the only possible opponent of error ; and it may be defended in the name of the law, as the unalienable right of all Englishmen.
